Maturity adjustment The progressive advance of the believer toward spiritual maturity through the daily intake of Bible doctrine via GAP. Culminates in cracking the maturity barrier and receiving the sixth imputation of divine blessing. Represents the second major adjustment to the justice of God in the plan of God.

Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five

Romans 13:1 — Introduction Continued: Divine Establishment, Human Freedom, and the Decalogue

Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Every soul must subordinate himself to superior authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and the existing authorities have been established by God.

Chapter thirteen of Romans has not yet received its verse-by-verse exegesis. The preceding sessions have been devoted to introducing the chapter through a systematic exposition of the doctrine of divine establishment. The present chapter continues that introduction, treating establishment and human freedom (points eight through eleven) and the relationship of the Decalogue to the laws of divine establishment (point nine). These doctrinal foundations govern the proper understanding of the believer's obligation to governmental authority in Romans 13:1–7.

I. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 8: Establishment and Human Freedom

Freedom is not a political abstraction but a theological reality grounded in the act of creation. When God prepared a human soul and imputed life to it, the capacity for freedom was simultaneously established. The soul's constituent functions — volition, mentality, emotion, conscience, and self-consciousness — are the faculties through which freedom is exercised. Freedom therefore exists as an extension of those functions.

Freedom operates in two distinct areas. The first is an extension of the imputation of human life at birth, which is the domain of the laws of divine establishment and applies to all people regardless of spiritual status. The second is an extension of the imputation of God's righteousness at salvation, which belongs to the believer alone and is governed by the principles of Bible doctrine and the royal family honor code. The laws of divine establishment protect the first area; the principles of the honor code develop the second.

Because man was created to resolve the angelic conflict, human freedom is an extension of that conflict into history. The laws of divine establishment are therefore designed to protect freedom so that evangelism and spiritual advance can occur in every generation. These laws protect the privacy, property, freedom, and individual volition of all people. The Decalogue — the Ten Commandments — is an integral part of this protective framework.

Biblical Witness to Human Freedom

Several key passages define the scope of freedom under divine establishment. Galatians 5:1 declares: "In the sphere of freedom Christ has freed us; stand firm therefore and stop being enmeshed by the yoke of slavery" — the slavery in view being not physical bondage but enslavement to legalism and to the evil system. John 8:32 anticipates the royal family honor code: knowledge of doctrine produces freedom. Romans 8:21 speaks of a future freedom, the freedom of glory belonging to the children of God. 2 Corinthians 3:17 locates spiritual freedom in the present ministry of the Holy Spirit: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Psalm 119:45 connects freedom to positive volition toward doctrine: "I will walk in freedom, for I seek Your doctrines" — the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) requires freedom in which to operate.

Establishment Freedom Distinguished from Spiritual Freedom

The spiritual freedom belonging to the believer must be carefully distinguished from establishment freedom, which is the heritage of all people within a national entity. Establishment freedom applies to believer and unbeliever alike. Its existence and perpetuation demand two things: respect for establishment authority, and a shared understanding of the legal and constitutional framework within which that authority operates. A national entity that fails to maintain this shared framework undermines the very freedom it was designed to protect.

The existence and perpetuation of freedom also demand self-discipline and self-sacrifice — not only when freedom is externally threatened, but when it is not internally understood. Military victory is one means by which national freedom and the laws of divine establishment are maintained. Under those laws, freedom demands responsibility from both believer and unbeliever alike. However, in Romans 13:1–7, the passage under examination, the responsibility for freedom under establishment principles is addressed specifically to the believer. The royal family honor code requires the Church Age believer to render to government the things that are government's and to God the things that are God's — including compliance with the nation's laws and, when necessary, its defense.

II. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 9: Establishment and the Decalogue

The Decalogue, or Ten Commandments, is filed primarily in Exodus 20:1–17. In the Hebrew text these commandments are introduced by the imperfect tense used as an imperative — the force of a categorical prohibition or mandate. The Decalogue does not have as its primary subject the cataloguing of sins. Its subject is human freedom. It just so happens that certain sins constitute attacks upon freedom, and at those points the two subjects converge. Essentially the Ten Commandments define human freedom in terms of three relationships: attitude toward God, attitude toward people, and attitude toward property.

The First Commandment — Exodus 20:3

"You shall have no other gods before Me." While this commandment obviously prohibits idolatry, its scope is considerably wider. At the level of divine establishment, it constitutes a national recognition that Jesus Christ controls history. A client nation that acknowledges this reality aligns itself with the source of its protection and blessing. A nation that abandons this recognition removes itself from the framework of divine blessing that sustains national freedom.

The Second Commandment — Exodus 20:4–6

The second commandment prohibits overt idolatry, defined in Scripture as contact with the demonic (Zechariah 10:2; 1 Corinthians 10:19–21). The distinction between the first and second commandments is the distinction between mental idolatry — substituting any person, system, or ideology for the recognition of God — and overt idolatry, the active practice of demon-influenced religion. Mental idolatry destroys individual freedom; overt idolatry destroys a nation, as demonstrated in the prophetic record (Isaiah 28; Isaiah 36:18–20; Isaiah 37:12–19; Jeremiah 3:6–11; Ezekiel 6:4–6).

The Third Commandment — Exodus 20:7

"You shall not use the name of the Lord your God for shav'" — the Hebrew term (שָׁוְא) means evil, worthlessness, or vanity. The commandment prohibits invoking the name of God as a cover for deception, false testimony, perjury, or manipulation. It is commonly misunderstood as referring only to profanity. While using God's name as a mere expletive does violate this commandment, the primary referent is the use of God's name to sponsor a lie — calling God as witness to a falsehood, or invoking divine authority to coerce a decision. God's name is properly used in worship, prayer, praise, thanksgiving, and doctrinal communication. It is not to be used as a front for theft, manipulation, or coercion.

The Fourth Commandment — Exodus 20:8–11

The Sabbath commandment relates human volition to time and establishes an economic principle under the laws of divine establishment: those who work must have adequate rest. The Sabbath mandates a full day of cessation from labor. This was a radical innovation in the ancient world, where no concept of a regular day off existed. The physiological and psychological necessity of a twenty-four-hour rest period was not understood; the Mosaic law mandated it as a matter of divine establishment. The man who has no rest becomes a slave to his labor and loses the capacity to exercise personal freedom. The Sabbath also carries a theological dimension: resting from work is a picture of grace — of receiving benefit without personal exertion — and was designed to point Israel to the grace of God. The faith-rest application of the Sabbath principle, treated elsewhere in the epistle, is distinct from this establishment function.

The Fifth Commandment — Exodus 20:12

"Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be prolonged in the land which the Lord your God gives you." This commandment establishes the principle that orientation to authority is the foundational pattern for all of life. The parents are the first authority encountered by the individual, and the child's response to parental authority determines the pattern of response to all subsequent authority structures. Orientation to legitimate authority is the basis for long life, stability, and national blessing. Resistance to authority, by contrast, produces a short, unstable, and ultimately destructive existence.

The Sixth Commandment — Exodus 20:13

"You shall not murder" — the corrected translation. The Hebrew term is רצח (ratsach), which denotes unlawful killing, not killing as such. Killing is divinely authorized in two contexts: the execution of capital punishment under the law, and the killing of enemy combatants in military service on behalf of one's national entity. Both are compatible with divine policy and the laws of divine establishment.

Murder, by contrast, is both a sin and the most fundamental violation of human freedom. When a person is murdered, every remaining opportunity to exercise freedom is permanently foreclosed. The divine prohibition of murder therefore protects the most basic condition of all other freedoms: the right to remain alive. God alone holds the prerogative over the timing of human death. Intrusion upon that prerogative through murder is simultaneously a sin, a violation of establishment law, and a presumption upon divine sovereignty. Of the seven most destructive sins identified in Proverbs 6:16–19, only one is an overt act: murder. The remaining six are attitudinal or verbal. This underscores that murder is the singular overt crime at the apex of anti-establishment behavior.

The Seventh Commandment — Exodus 20:14

"You shall not commit adultery." Adultery, like murder, is simultaneously a sin and an attack on human freedom. It specifically violates the freedom of the right man–right woman relationship — the divinely designed pairing that provides the highest expression of category two love. The seventh commandment is addressed primarily to the man, consistent with the ancient world's recognition that the husband is the guardian of the marriage bond. Adultery distorts and destroys the capacity for genuine love, substituting predatory exploitation for the covenant relationship. The woman as right woman belongs to one right man; she is not the property of multiple partners. The commandment thus protects the institution of marriage as the structural unit in which category two love is properly expressed and sustained.

The Eighth Commandment — Exodus 20:15

"You shall not steal." The eighth commandment establishes the right of private property under the laws of divine establishment and demands that government protect both the lives and the possessions of those within a national entity. Stealing is simultaneously a sin, a crime, and a fundamental disorientation to life. It represents the failure to recognize that what belongs to another person is categorically off-limits, regardless of circumstances. The believer who has absorbed doctrine into the soul can walk past any object belonging to another person — however valuable — without the slightest impulse to appropriate it. This orientation is not merely a function of legal compliance but of settled respect for the establishment principle that property is an extension of freedom.

The eighth commandment also has a macroeconomic application. Confiscatory taxation beyond the scriptural ceiling of ten percent constitutes governmental theft. When a government systematically appropriates legitimate profits and private wealth under ideological cover, it violates the same establishment principle the commandment was designed to protect. The socialist premise that wealth should be redistributed for the greater good is a direct violation of the eighth commandment at the national level.

The Ninth Commandment — Exodus 20:16

"You shall not answer as a false witness against your neighbor." The ninth commandment protects human freedom through the objectivity of the legal process. The judicial system cannot function without truthful testimony; hearsay and perjury, when admitted as evidence, transform the courtroom from an instrument of justice into an instrument of oppression. The same principle extends beyond the courtroom: gossip and maligning — spreading falsehoods about another person outside a legal context — are verbal violations of this establishment principle. Verbal sins are always sinful, but this verbal sin is additionally anti-establishment because it undermines the social fabric of trust upon which freedom depends. The standard of live-and-let-live cannot be maintained in a society where false testimony — legal or social — goes unchecked.

The Tenth Commandment — Exodus 20:17

"You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's." The tenth commandment demands restraint of the lust pattern of the old sin nature under the principle of live-and-let-live. Significantly, this commandment was the instrument through which the Apostle Paul came to recognize the true nature of the old sin nature, as he recounts in Romans 7:7: "I would not have known sin except through the law, for I would not have known about coveting if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet.'" Covetousness — epithymia (ἐπιθυμία) — is the craving for what belongs to another, whether property, position, relationships, or status. It is the internal disposition that, if unchecked, drives theft, adultery, and murder. The tenth commandment therefore strikes at the root of all anti-establishment behavior by demanding restraint at the level of desire itself.

III. Summary: The Decalogue as the Framework of Human Freedom

The Ten Commandments, taken together, constitute a coherent framework for the protection of human freedom across three domains: the relationship between the individual and God (commandments one through four), the relationship between individuals (commandments five through seven and nine through ten), and the relationship of the individual to property (commandments eight and ten). This framework is not confined to Israel under the Mosaic covenant. The underlying establishment principles — that God governs history, that life must be protected, that property is sacred, that testimony must be truthful, that desire must be disciplined — are universal and apply to every national entity in every age.

For the Church Age believer, these establishment principles are integrated into the royal family honor code. Compliance with them is not optional moralism but a component of the believer's responsibility within the Protocol Plan of God. Romans 13:1–7 will demonstrate that the specific application of these principles to the believer's relationship with governing authorities flows directly from this foundation. The exegesis of the passage itself will begin in the following session.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five

1. Freedom is grounded in creation, not in political theory. When God imputed human life to the soul, He simultaneously established the capacity for freedom. The soul's functions — volition, mentality, conscience, emotion, self-consciousness — are the faculties through which freedom is exercised. Freedom is therefore a theological datum before it is a political one.

2. Freedom operates in two areas governed by different principles. Establishment freedom, grounded in the imputation of human life at birth, belongs to all people and is protected by the laws of divine establishment. Spiritual freedom, grounded in the imputation of God's righteousness at salvation, belongs to the believer alone and is developed through the principles of Bible doctrine and the royal family honor code.

3. The Decalogue defines human freedom, not primarily human sin. The Ten Commandments are a comprehensive framework for the protection of freedom across three relational domains: the individual's relationship to God, to other persons, and to property. Where sin is also addressed, it is because certain sins constitute attacks upon freedom.

4. The first commandment requires national recognition that Jesus Christ controls history. Idolatry — whether mental (substituting any ideology or person for God) or overt (demon-influenced religion) — destroys the theological basis for national survival. The prophetic record uniformly demonstrates that idolatry leads to national collapse.

5. God's name is properly used only in worship, prayer, praise, and doctrinal communication. Using God's name as a cover for lying, manipulation, or coercion violates the third commandment. The most egregious form of this violation is invoking divine authority to compel a decision or sponsor a falsehood.

6. The Sabbath establishes an economic principle: those who labor must have adequate rest. A full day of rest is not merely a religious observance but an establishment requirement. The person who has no rest becomes enslaved to his labor and loses the capacity to exercise freedom in other domains of life.

7. Murder is the singular overt act at the apex of anti-establishment behavior. Of the seven most destructive sins, only murder is an overt act. It permanently forecloses every remaining freedom of the victim and constitutes a presumption upon the divine prerogative over the timing of death. Military killing and capital punishment are divinely authorized and are not violations of the sixth commandment.

8. The right to private property is a divine establishment principle. The eighth commandment demands that government protect private property and prohibits confiscation under any ideological cover. Covetousness — the internal lust for another's possessions — is addressed by the tenth commandment, which strikes at the root of theft, adultery, and social disorder by demanding restraint at the level of desire.

9. Truthful testimony is an establishment requirement, not merely a moral preference. The ninth commandment demands objectivity in the legal process by prohibiting false witness. The same principle governs social discourse: gossip and maligning are anti-establishment violations that destroy the trust upon which freedom depends.

10. The believer's obligation to authority structures is not optional. The royal family honor code requires the Church Age believer to recognize and submit to legitimate authority — governmental, parental, legal — as part of the Protocol Plan of God. Romans 13:1–7 applies this foundational establishment doctrine directly to the believer's relationship with governing authorities. The verse-by-verse exegesis of that passage will proceed in the following session.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
Divine Establishment The set of universal divine institutions and laws — including individual volition, marriage, family, and national government — designed to protect human freedom so that evangelism and spiritual advance can occur in every generation. These laws apply to believer and unbeliever alike.
epithymia ἐπιθυμία epithymia — craving, coveting, lust Strong desire or craving directed toward what belongs to another. Used in Romans 7:7 as the specific sin that the tenth commandment addresses. The inner disposition underlying theft, adultery, and social disorder. Distinguished from legitimate desire by its orientation toward the property or relationships of another.
ratsach רָצַח ratsach — to murder, to slay unlawfully Hebrew verb used in the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13). Denotes unlawful killing — murder — as distinct from killing authorized by law (capital punishment) or warfare. The commandment's corrected translation is 'You shall not murder,' not 'You shall not kill.'
shav' שָׁוְא shav' — vanity, evil, worthlessness Hebrew noun used in the third commandment (Exodus 20:7). Denotes that which is empty, false, or wicked. The commandment prohibits using God's name for shav' — invoking divine authority as a cover for deception, perjury, or manipulation. Not limited to profanity; primarily addresses the misuse of God's name to sponsor falsehood.
GAP Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received, transferred from the human spirit to the right lobe of the soul, and converted into epignosis — full, exact knowledge available for application. Requires the filling of the Holy Spirit and consistent intake of accurately taught doctrine.
epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignosis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for spiritual growth and application. Distinguished from gnosis (surface or academic knowledge) in that epignosis has been transferred to the right lobe of the soul and is operational. Doctrine must reach the level of epignosis to function in the believer's life.
Old Sin Nature (OSN) The sin capacity inherited at birth through the male genetic line, transmitted from Adam. Contains both a lust pattern (driving toward various forms of excess and desire) and an area of weakness producing personal sin. The tenth commandment — 'You shall not covet' — was the instrument through which Paul recognized the full extent of the old sin nature's operation (Romans 7:7).
Royal Family Honor Code The operational standard governing the Church Age believer as a member of the royal family of God. Encompasses the believer's responsibilities to God, to other persons, and to national entities, including submission to governmental authority (Romans 13:1–7). Integrates establishment principles with the higher demands of the spiritual life unique to the Church Age.
Client Nation A national entity that God uses as a base for the communication of the gospel, the teaching of Bible doctrine, and the support of missionary activity. A client nation is characterized by a pivot of mature believers, respect for the laws of divine establishment, and freedom of religious expression. Client nation status is forfeited through sustained negative volition and violation of establishment principles.

Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Six

Romans 13:1 — Christian Responsibility to Government; Divine Establishment and Governing Authorities

Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: All human beings, be subordinating yourselves to governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and the existing authorities have been appointed by God.

Romans 13 opens the fourth major block of practical doctrine in the epistle. Having established the doctrinal framework of adjustment to the justice of God through chapters 1–11, and having called for the believer's presentation to God as a living sacrifice in 12:1–2, Paul now addresses a triad of civic responsibilities: to government (13:1–7), to others in the human race (13:8–10), and to oneself as a member of the royal family of God (13:11–14). Chapter 386 covers the concluding section of the Doctrine of Divine Establishment as developed across this lecture series, specifically the principle of morality under establishment, and then opens the exegesis of 13:1 with the foundational command of subordination to governing authorities.

I. The Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Morality (Points 10–13)

The Ten Commandments, surveyed in previous sessions, define morality in terms of divine establishment. This section completes the doctrinal framework with points on the nature, scope, and limits of morality before moving to the exegesis of Romans 13:1.

Point 10 — Morality Defined within Establishment

Morality is right conduct and excellence in the practice and function of the laws of divine establishment. It is the observation of those laws. Because the laws of divine establishment govern the entire human race — not the Church alone — morality is commanded of believer and unbeliever alike. Sin in any of its forms constitutes an attack on establishment; morality is the ordered response and antidote to that attack.

Several implications follow directly. First, morality is not Christianity. Whatever is commanded of the unbeliever is not the Christian way of life as such, since the unbeliever cannot fulfill the specifically Christian requirements. Second, morality is not the monopoly of Christianity. Any member of the human race who understands and complies with the standards of divine establishment can function morally — without the filling of the Holy Spirit, without the intake of Bible doctrine, and without a personal relationship with the Lord Jesus Christ. Third, the equation of morality with Christianity is a category error that produces a false standard: the notion that keeping a simplified moral code constitutes the Christian way of life or qualifies one for eternal salvation.

Point 11 — The Christian Way of Life Exceeds Morality

The Christian way of life is not morality. It consists of the following:

(a) The filling of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). (b) Maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). (c) Positive volition toward doctrine. (d) Maturity adjustment to the justice of God. (e) Functioning under the royal family honor code. (f) Advancing through the maturity barrier to supergrace and ultra-supergrace.

None of these elements can be accomplished by the unbeliever. The unbeliever is commanded morality; the believer is commanded morality and infinitely more. Morality is the floor, not the ceiling, of the Christian life. To mistake the floor for the ceiling is reversionism.

Point 12 — Morality Protects Freedom but Does Not Produce Salvation

Morality, as an establishment factor, protects human freedom. It does not provide eternal salvation. This distinction is explicitly established in the following passages: Romans 3:20; Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16; Titus 3:5. Morality cannot produce the filling of the Spirit, cannot learn doctrine, and cannot advance the believer to maturity. These are the exclusive province of the Christian way of life.

Point 13 — Morality Provides the Environment for the Function of Christianity

Morality can and does protect human freedom. Believers are protected by the moral fabric of the society in which they live. A morally ordered society provides the environment of freedom required for evangelism, for Bible teaching, and for the correct function of the local church. Immorality, by contrast, produces anarchy — the collapse of authority — and in that collapse the conditions necessary for the believer's spiritual advance are destroyed.

Christian dynamics therefore includes morality but at the same time exceeds morality. Morality is the environment in which Christianity can function; Christianity is not morality. The mature believer is neither anti-establishment nor immoral. Compliance with establishment doctrines and authority is a morality function; compliance with the royal family honor code is a distinctively Christian function. Both are required. Neither replaces the other.

The privatization of industry, the destruction of property rights, and the suppression of human freedom — characteristic of every form of collectivist statism — are concrete expressions of immorality in the establishment sense. Socialism in all its forms is anti-establishment and therefore immoral, because it denies the individual the product of his own labor and substitutes coercive redistribution for freely exercised right to property. The distinction between property rights and human rights is false: all rights are human rights, and property rights are among the most ancient and essential of them.

II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts

Three passages define the Christian's civic obligations under divine establishment:

Matthew 22:21: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Our Lord here delineates two sets of standards, both designed by God: the laws of divine establishment (civic responsibility) and the royal family honor code (responsibility to God). They are not in conflict; they are complementary obligations operating at different levels.

1 Timothy 2:1–2: Paul directs prayer on behalf of kings and all in authority, "in order that we may lead undisturbed and tranquil lives in all godliness." Tranquil civic life is the precondition for the assembly of believers to receive doctrine. Godliness here refers to spiritual maturity and integrity — the function of the royal family honor code under the daily intake of doctrine.

1 Peter 2:13–14: "Subordinate yourselves for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether to a king as one in authority or to a governor sent by him for the punishment of those who do evil or the recognition of those who do good." The basis of submission is not the personal character of the ruler but the Lord's own sanction of human government as a divine institution.

III. Outline of Romans 13

Romans 13 develops Christian responsibility along three axes:

Paragraph 1 (vv. 1–7): Christian responsibility to government.

Paragraph 2 (vv. 8–10): Christian responsibility to others — the rest of the human race.

Paragraph 3 (vv. 11–14): Christian responsibility to oneself as a member of the royal family of God.

The three paragraphs form a coherent unit. The believer exists simultaneously in a civic order, a social order, and a spiritual order. Each imposes legitimate claims. The doctrine of divine establishment addresses all three.

IV. Exegesis of Romans 13:1a — The Command of Subordination

Vocative Address: 'All Human Beings'

The verse opens with a vocative address constructed from two forms: the adjective pas (πᾶς), meaning all, and the noun psychē (ψυχή), vocative feminine singular. The noun psychē carries three related meanings: (1) soul, (2) life — since the soul is the residence of human life, and (3) human being — since human existence is constituted by the divine imputation of life to the divinely prepared soul at birth. In this context the third meaning is primary. The address is therefore: All human beings — every person who has received the imputation of human life, believer and unbeliever alike.

Main Verb: hupotassō — 'Be Subordinating Yourselves'

The main verb is the present middle imperative of hupotassō (ὑποτάσσω). The term is a military compound: hypo (under) + tassō (to arrange in order). It means to subordinate oneself to authority and carries the force of ordered, voluntary alignment within a command structure.

Three features of the verbal form are exegetically significant:

(1) Present tense (progressive): Linear, continuous action. Subordination to authority is not a single act but a sustained posture of life — a permanent orientation of the will.

(2) Middle voice (direct reflexive): The action is referred directly back to the agent with reflexive force. The subject subordinates himself — the emphasis falls on self-discipline and voluntary cognizance of authority, not on external coercion.

(3) Imperative mood: This is a command addressed to the entire human race. Subordination to governing authority is not a suggestion, a cultural accommodation, or a uniquely Jewish or Christian obligation. It is a universal moral requirement grounded in the laws of divine establishment.

Object: 'To Governing Authorities'

The dative plural indirect object consists of two elements. First, the present active participle of hyperechō (ὑπερέχω), used as an adjective modifying the noun. The participle does not mean simply "higher" but governing — it denotes duly constituted authority under divine institution number four (human government). Second, the noun exousia (ἐξουσία) in the dative plural: authorities. Corrected translation of the first phrase: All human beings, be subordinating yourselves to governing authorities.

V. Historical and Isagogical Background

The command addresses two groups of readers in Rome whose errors required correction.

Jewish Christians in Rome had distorted Deuteronomy 17:15, which restricts the appointment of foreign kings over Israel, into a general warrant for disobeying the Roman civil order. Their argument was that subordination to Caesar was spiritually impermissible. Paul himself, also Jewish, was subordinate to Caesar throughout his ministry — including when that subordination ultimately cost him his life. He understood what the reversionistic Jewish Christians in Rome did not: Deuteronomy 17:15 addresses theocratic Israel's internal governance and carries no warrant for civic insubordination under human government in the Church Age.

Gentile Christians in Rome had adopted a different error: the position that a morally compromised ruler forfeits his claim to obedience. This reasoning — however intuitive it may seem — collapses the distinction between authority as a principle and the personal character of the one who holds authority. The personal sins of a ruler do not dissolve the divine sanction of the office, unless his conduct involves criminal activity that destroys the integrity of the authority itself. Personal morality is an issue the individual applies to himself; it is not the criterion by which one evaluates the validity of governing authority. Julius Caesar and Napoleon Bonaparte are cited in the lecture as historical illustrations of rulers whose personal conduct was morally irregular yet who advanced the cause of ordered, law-governed freedom in ways that moral rulers sometimes failed to do.

At the time Paul wrote, Nero held the office of Caesar. Some Roman Christians were involved in or sympathetic to revolutionary activity on the grounds that Nero's tyranny justified resistance. The word of God says no. Revolution replaces duly constituted authority by means of violence, and the violence employed invariably produces a worse tyranny than the one it displaced. The French Revolution is the paradigm case: the violence used to overthrow the Bourbon monarchy generated the Terror, and the liberty promised by the revolutionaries proved far more destructive of human freedom than the regime they removed. There was no American Revolution in this sense — the War for Independence was a war for the preservation and legal vindication of already-existing rights, not the violent imposition of a new order by a revolutionary vanguard.

Paul's clarification is therefore addressed simultaneously to reversionistic Jewish distortion of Scripture, to Gentile moralism applied wrongly to the question of authority, and to incipient revolutionary sentiment among Roman believers. The answer to all three errors is the same: the laws of divine establishment require subordination to governing authority, and that requirement holds regardless of the personal morality or political acceptability of the one who governs.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Six

1. Morality is not Christianity. It is the human race functioning under the laws of divine establishment. Any member of the human race — believer or unbeliever — can be moral. Morality requires neither the filling of the Spirit, the intake of doctrine, nor a personal relationship with God. It is commanded of both believer and unbeliever alike.

2. The Christian way of life exceeds morality. It consists of the filling of the Spirit, maximum doctrine resident in the soul through the daily function of GAP, positive volition toward doctrine, functioning under the royal family honor code, and advancing to maturity adjustment to the justice of God. None of these can be accomplished by the unbeliever.

3. Morality protects human freedom but cannot produce salvation. This is the consistent teaching of Romans 3:20, 3:28, Galatians 2:16, and Titus 3:5. Morality is the floor of ordered human society; Christianity is the superstructure built upon that floor.

4. Morality provides the environment for the function of Christianity. A morally ordered society under duly constituted authority creates the conditions of freedom in which believers can assemble, receive doctrine, and advance spiritually. Immorality produces anarchy and destroys those conditions.

5. The command of Romans 13:1 is addressed to all human beings without distinction. The vocative address — all human beings — makes clear that subordination to governing authority is a universal moral requirement of divine establishment, not a distinctively Christian or Jewish obligation.

6. The verb hupotassō is a military term denoting voluntary, self-disciplined subordination. The middle voice emphasizes that the subject subordinates himself — the action flows from cognizance of authority and disciplined will, not from external compulsion. The progressive present indicates that this is a sustained, continuous posture of life.

7. The personal morality of a ruler does not determine the validity of his authority. The divine institution of human government stands independently of the character of the person who holds office. Personal sins of a ruler are a matter between him and God; they do not constitute a warrant for disobedience or revolutionary activity by those governed.

8. Revolution is not a permissible response to tyranny under the laws of divine establishment. Violence used to overthrow duly constituted authority invariably produces a worse tyranny than the one displaced. The French Revolution is the paradigm. The legitimate means of redress under establishment are law, due process, elections, and the formation of a mature pivot of believers whose adjustment to the justice of God stabilizes the nation.

9. Two Jewish and Gentile errors in Rome required correction. Jewish Christians distorted Deuteronomy 17:15 into a warrant for disobeying Caesar. Gentile Christians made the personal morality of the ruler the criterion for obedience. Both errors confuse separate categories: the first confuses theocratic Israel's internal law with Church Age civic obligation; the second confuses personal character with the divine sanction of authority as an institution.

10. Governing authorities translates the dative plural of exousia modified by the participle hyperechō. The participle means governing — duly constituted authority — not merely superior in rank. The combined phrase identifies human government as divine institution number four, ordained by God for the ordered preservation of human freedom.

Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Seven

Romans 13:1 — Divine Establishment, Delegated Authority, and the Prohibition of Revolution

Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: All human beings subordinate yourselves to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except delegated by God, and the existing authorities have been established by God.

Romans 13:1 stands at the intersection of Christian theology and political philosophy. Paul wrote these words in AD 58, eight years before the Jewish revolution of AD 66 — a revolution his instruction in this verse was designed to forestall. The chapter addresses the relationship of the believer, and indeed of every human being, to civil government as an expression of divine establishment. This chapter completes the exegesis of the first phrase of verse 1 and then turns to the explanatory clause that follows: 'For there is no authority except delegated by God.'

I. Summary of the First Phrase: 'All Human Beings Subordinate Yourselves to Governing Authorities'

The opening imperative of Romans 13:1 is addressed without restriction to all human beings — believers and unbelievers alike. The following points summarize the exegetical and doctrinal content established in prior study of this phrase.

1. Membership in the royal family of God does not exempt the believer from the responsibility of submission to authority under the laws of divine establishment. Christians are not exempt from military training, civic responsibility, obedience to law, or taxation. Believers are as fully involved in the function of civil society as unbelievers.

2. Neither anarchy nor revolution is ever condoned or sanctioned by the Word of God.

3. Historical background — the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius (AD 51). The emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because their distortion of Messianic eschatology had issued in active rejection of Roman governmental authority. The Roman Empire provided Jews with legal protection, freedom of movement, freedom to observe their laws and customs, and freedom of commerce throughout the empire. Yet a significant segment of the Jewish community distorted biblical eschatology into a rationale for non-participation in and rejection of Roman governance. They argued that Messianic expectation relieved them of any obligation to the governing power. The Word of God does not support that conclusion.

4. The distortion of Messianic eschatology does not eliminate civic responsibility. Anticipation of the return of Christ does not relieve the believer of the obligation to render to civil authority what civil authority is owed — including taxes, military service, and civic participation. Submission to authority is not contingent on the moral quality of the authority or on one's eschatological expectations.

5. This distortion of Jewish eschatology eventuated in the Jewish revolution of AD 66. The spirit of revolution, already present in Judaism when Paul wrote Romans in AD 58, culminated eight years later in open revolt during the reign of Nero. The result was the administration of the fifth cycle of discipline to the southern kingdom of Judea: the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the nation in AD 70. It was God's will for the Jewish people to remain under Roman authority and to utilize the freedom that Rome provided. Their rejection of that authority led to catastrophic destruction. The violence they initiated was returned to them many times over — siege, starvation, internecine slaughter, and mass death — demonstrating that those who resort to violence to solve political problems invite violence as their answer.

6. Romans 13 was written eight years before the revolution and twenty-two years before the fall of Jerusalem. Paul was already dead when the revolution culminated in AD 70. His instruction in this chapter, had it been heeded, would have prevented the disaster entirely.

7. Paul wrote Romans 13 while Nero sat on the imperial throne. Nero was a degenerate ruler — vicious, immoral, and ultimately the instrument of Paul's own execution by decapitation. Yet Paul does not advocate revolution against Nero. He does not qualify his submission to governing authorities by the moral character of the ruler. The office and the authority it carries are divinely established regardless of the character of the individual occupying that office.

8. Revolutionary fanaticism is forbidden by the Word of God. What doctrine cannot solve is not solvable by human revolution. This is a controlling principle: the believer's instrument of social transformation is the intake and application of Bible doctrine, not political violence or conspiracy.

9. Even slaves in the Roman Empire were commanded not to revolt. Christian slaves were commanded to remain in their status and to honor the authority structure over them. God's plan for the life of a Christian slave was not hindered by the fact of slavery. The slave who was advancing in doctrine and in personal relationship to God was functioning within the Protocol Plan of God regardless of his legal status. This demonstrates the sufficiency of doctrine to provide genuine inner freedom in any external circumstance.

10. Assassination of a ruler or the violent overthrow of government is not the prerogative of the believer in Jesus Christ. Christianity is never to be involved in conspiratorial violence against civil authority. The believer's weapons are not carnal.

11. As with individuals, so with nations: leave judgment, punitive action, and discipline to the Lord. Revolution is an intrusion on the prerogative of the justice of God, just as gossip, maligning, judging, and backbiting are intrusions on that same prerogative at the personal level.

12. Revolution is collective presumption — collective blasphemy. While gossip, maligning, and judging constitute personal presumption against the justice of God, revolution constitutes collective presumption. Both are forbidden; the collective form is the more serious offense by reason of its scale.

13. The erosion of political freedom does not eliminate the believer's most important freedom. The freedom to worship, to receive Bible doctrine, to assemble for teaching, and to exercise positive volition toward the Word of God has not been revoked. This freedom — the freedom to take in doctrine — is the one freedom that can reverse the course of a nation. Since the Lord Jesus Christ controls history, a sufficiently large pivot of mature believers changes the historical trajectory of a nation. God honors the pivot and uses it as His instrument of historical course correction.

14. While many principles contrary to divine establishment have been adopted by modern governments, the command of Romans 13:1 remains in force. The believer is still under the obligation to recognize the authority of civil government. The theological and moral failures of a government do not dissolve that obligation.

15. Civil government is necessary under the laws of divine establishment. Revolt and anarchy are simultaneously anti-God, anti-human, and destructive of the very freedom they claim to seek. Anarchy does not produce freedom; it produces tyranny. Every successful modern revolution has demonstrated the same pattern: middle-class aspirations for recognition initiate the destruction of existing authority structures, and the resulting anarchy is filled by a tyrant worse than the ruler deposed.

16. The principle of authority requires respect for the office, not necessarily for the character or personality of the one holding it. There may be a bad president, a bad local official, a corrupt police officer, or an unjust tax collector — none of these facts eliminates the authority that the office itself carries. The believer submits to the office and the principle it represents, not to the personal virtue or competence of the individual occupying it.

17. Where authority is the issue, the personality and character of the authority cannot simultaneously be the issue. This principle applies across every sphere of authority: civil government, military command, employer-employee relations, the marriage relationship, the parent-child relationship, the coach-athlete relationship, and the pastor-congregation relationship. When submission to authority is required, the personal qualities of the authority figure are not the operative consideration. The principle of authority itself is the operative consideration.

18. The personality and character of the husband is not the issue in marital authority. A husband's authority in the marriage relationship resides in the fact that he is the husband, not in the fact that he is always pleasant, always kind, or always correct. No human authority is infallible. The principle of authority remains valid even when the person exercising it makes errors in judgment.

19. The personality and character of the parents is not the issue in parental authority. Parental authority resides in the fact of parenthood, not in the congeniality of the parent's manner. Firm and consistent discipline, even when resented in the moment, is among the most important gifts a parent can provide.

20. The personality and character of the employer is not the issue in vocational authority. An employee may legitimately dislike the personality of a supervisor or disagree with managerial decisions, but the authority structure of the workplace is a reflection of divine establishment and is to be honored on that basis.

21. The personality and character of the coach is not the issue in athletic or institutional authority. The same principle extends to every institutional authority relationship. Demanding authority, properly exercised, produces capacity and discipline that voluntary instruction alone cannot produce.

22. The personality and character of the pastor is not the issue in ecclesiastical authority. The pastor-teacher's authority in the local church resides in the spiritual gift of pastor-teacher and in the congregation's acceptance of his teaching ministry, not in the personal attractiveness or perfection of the individual. The content of the teaching, not the personality of the teacher, is the operative consideration.

23. The personality and character of the president of the United States is not the issue in civil authority. The authority of the office of president resides in the constitutional order, not in the moral stature or policy wisdom of the individual elected to that office. The believer may disagree with policy, may engage in loyal opposition, and may advocate through lawful means for different courses of action — but submission to the authority of the office itself is not optional.

24. The personality and character of the tax authority is not the issue. The tax collector's authority resides in the fact that he functions as an instrument of the civil government, which itself operates under delegated divine authority. Submission to taxation is commanded by Scripture regardless of whether the tax system is just, equitable, or well administered.

25. The personality and character of the police officer is not the issue. Law enforcement authority resides in the office, not the individual. The believer respects and cooperates with the authority of law enforcement as an expression of submission to divine establishment.

II. Exegesis of the Explanatory Clause: 'For There Is No Authority Except Delegated by God'

Having established the scope of the imperative, Paul provides the theological ground for the command. The explanatory clause is introduced by the post-positive conjunctive particle and proceeds with a static present indicative of negated existence, followed by a predicate nominative and a prepositional phrase indicating source.

A. The Explanatory Particle

The clause opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), used here in its explanatory function: for. This particle signals that what follows is not a separate assertion but the theological ground of the preceding imperative. The command to subordinate oneself to governing authorities is not merely a prudential or sociological observation — it rests on a theological reality about the nature and source of all authority.

B. The Verb and Its Negation

The present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί) with the negative ou (οὐ) asserts a condition assumed to be perpetually existing. The present tense here is a static present: it describes a state of affairs that is constant and permanent under the laws of divine establishment. Ou is used rather than mē because the indicative mood is in view — this is a declarative, objective, dogmatic statement of doctrine, not a condition or subjunctive possibility.

C. The Predicate Nominative: exousia

The predicate nominative singular is exousia (ἐξουσία), meaning authority — and specifically delegated authority. This is the same term used in the opening imperative of verse 1. Exousia in the New Testament carries the sense of rightful, recognized, officially granted power — authority that comes from a source above the one exercising it. The statement is absolute: there is no authority — no exousia of any kind, in any sphere, at any level — that does not derive from God.

D. The Prepositional Phrase: Source and Origin

The prepositional phrase hupo (ὑπό) plus the ablative of theos (θεός) indicates source or origin. When hupo governs the ablative case, it specifies the ultimate source from which something proceeds. The full force of the construction is: except delegated by God. God is the origin and source of the entire system of authority that operates under the laws of divine establishment. Civil authority, parental authority, vocational authority, ecclesiastical authority — all derive their legitimacy from the authority of God Himself.

E. Doctrinal Synthesis

The full translation of the verse to this point reads: 'All human beings subordinate yourselves to governing authorities, for there is no authority except delegated by God.'

The theological logic is as follows. Because all authority originates with God, submission to legitimate authority is submission to a divinely established order. Conversely, revolt against that authority is revolt against God's established order — not merely a political act but a theological one. This is why Paul can command submission to Nero without qualification: the issue is not the moral quality of the ruler but the divinely established nature of the institution over which he presides.

A person may be entirely correct in their assessment that a particular law is unjust, that a particular ruler is corrupt, or that a particular policy is harmful. But the moment that correct assessment is deployed as a justification for bucking authority, the rightness of the position becomes secondary to the wrongness of the method. Authority takes precedence over the individual's assessment of what is right. This is not because human authority is infallible — it is not — but because the principle of authority itself, as a divinely established reality, is prior to and more fundamental than any particular judgment about the competence or virtue of the one exercising it.

All freedom exists because of authority. Anarchy does not produce freedom — it destroys freedom. The consistent pattern of history is that when authority structures are overthrown by revolutionary violence, the resulting vacuum is filled not by the liberty the revolutionaries promised but by a tyranny more oppressive than the one displaced. The laws of divine establishment exist precisely to prevent this outcome. When believers honor those laws — through submission, through doctrine, through building the national pivot of mature believers — God can and does alter the historical trajectory of a nation through means that no revolution could achieve.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Seven

1. Romans 13:1 addresses all human beings without exception. The command to subordinate oneself to governing authorities is not restricted to believers — it reflects the universal applicability of the laws of divine establishment to the entire human race.

2. The explanatory particle gar establishes the theological ground of the imperative. The reason submission to civil authority is commanded is that all authority is delegated by God. Submission to human authority is therefore an expression of submission to the divine order.

3. The static present indicative of the negated eimi expresses a permanent, perpetual truth. The non-existence of any authority apart from God's delegation is not a contingent historical observation — it is a permanent theological reality under the laws of divine establishment.

4. Exousia denotes delegated authority — authority that derives its legitimacy from a source above itself. No human authority is self-grounding. Every sphere of human authority — civil, domestic, vocational, ecclesiastical — participates in and depends upon the ultimate authority of God.

5. The preposition hupo with the ablative of theos specifies God as the ultimate source and origin of all delegated authority. This construction makes the theological claim as strong as possible: God is not merely the endorser of human authority structures — He is their origin.

6. The correctness of a grievance does not authorize revolt. A person may be entirely right in identifying an injustice, a corrupt official, or a harmful policy. But deploying that correct assessment as justification for bucking authority transforms a legitimate grievance into an illegitimate method. The principle of authority is prior to the individual's assessment of what is right.

7. Anarchy destroys the freedom it claims to seek. Every major modern revolution has followed the same pattern: the destruction of existing authority produces a vacuum that is filled by tyranny more severe than the regime overthrown. This is not a historical accident — it is the predictable consequence of violating the divinely established principle of authority.

8. The believer's instrument of social and historical transformation is Bible doctrine, not political violence. The pivot of mature believers — those who have advanced through the maturity barrier by sustained doctrine intake — is the means by which God alters the historical course of nations. No revolution has ever produced what the pivot produces: genuine, lasting, divinely blessed freedom.

9. The moral character of the ruler does not determine the validity of the authority the ruler exercises. Paul commanded submission to governing authority while Nero sat on the throne. The character of the individual occupying an office of authority is not the grounds on which the authority of that office stands or falls.

10. The principle of authority extends to every sphere of human life. Civil government, military command, employment, marriage, parenthood, athletic and educational institutions, and the local church all operate within divinely established authority structures. Where authority is the issue, the personality and character of the authority figure cannot simultaneously be the issue. The principle must be honored independent of the person administering it.
