Chapter Four Hundred Five

Romans 13:9 — The Decalogue as Criminal Law: Adultery, Murder, Theft, Perjury, and Covetousness

Romans 13:9 “For the commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, You shall not covet,' and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For instance, this: thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not murder, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not give false testimony, thou shalt not lust or covet. And if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word, namely, you shall love the other believer as yourself.

Romans 13:9 continues the argument that began in verse 8, where Paul established that impersonal love for one's neighbor fulfills the Mosaic Law. Here Paul specifies which commandments he has in mind: five prohibitions drawn from the Decalogue, each representing an attack upon human freedom that the laws of divine establishment are designed to restrain. The order of the commandments follows neither the Hebrew sequence of Exodus 20 nor the Septuagint exactly, but corresponds to the order found in Luke 18:20 and James 2:11, an order organized around the twin themes of human freedom under establishment and the honor code of the royal family of God.

The verse opens with the explanatory post-positive conjunctive particle γάρ (gar), translated 'for instance' here, linking what follows to the principle of verse 8. The nominative neuter singular of the definite article functions as a demonstrative pronoun — 'this' — pointing specifically to that portion of the Mosaic Law pertaining to criminal activity. The passage therefore moves from the broader ethical horizon of love-as-law-fulfillment to the concrete domain of crime as an assault upon freedom.

I. The Decalogue as the Magna Carta of Freedom

When this chapter opened, the Decalogue was introduced as the magna carta of human freedom. Freedom, privacy, and property are inseparable under the laws of divine establishment: remove any one of the three and the others collapse. Crime, by definition, is an assault upon all three simultaneously. The criminal invades privacy, destroys or seizes property, and negates the conditions under which freedom can be exercised. The five commandments quoted in verse 9 are not arbitrary moral prohibitions; they are the legal barriers that protect the social order in which human freedom can exist.

Each commandment listed in verse 9 describes conduct that is both a sin and a crime. The two categories are distinct but not mutually exclusive. All crimes are sins, but not all sins are crimes. The individual who is technically law-abiding may still be an unpleasant and destructive presence — self-righteous, judgmental, imposing personal taboos on others. Such a person has kept the law in its criminal prohibitions while failing entirely in the impersonal love requirement of verse 8. Verse 9 addresses the criminal dimension specifically; verse 8 addresses the broader ethical demand.

Two restraints operate simultaneously in this passage. First, the laws of divine establishment apply to the entire human race, believer and unbeliever alike. Morality — conformity to establishment law — is the minimum requirement for the preservation of civil order. Second, the royal family honor code applies to believers specifically and demands more. The believer is not merely restrained from crime because he recognizes the authority of establishment; he is restrained because he belongs to the royal family of God and because more is expected of him. Morality is not the Christian way of life, but morality is included within it.

II. Thou Shalt Not Commit Adultery

The first commandment cited is the prohibition of adultery. The Greek verb is μοιχεύω (moicheuō), future active indicative with the negative ού (ou). The future tense functions as an imperative — the imperative future, a construction found throughout classical Greek and not a Hebraism. Since the command necessarily involves futurity, the future indicative with the negative expresses the prohibition directly and forcefully. The human race produces the action; the emphasis within the passage falls on the believer as a member of the royal family of God.

Adultery must be distinguished from fornication. Fornication — πορνεία (porneia) — is illicit sexual activity in its various forms; it is a sin. Adultery is a subset of fornication but carries an additional dimension: it is also a crime, because it involves theft. Marriage establishes a legally recognized property relationship. A married woman is the legal property of her husband under the framework of biblical law and ancient Near Eastern jurisprudence alike. When a man seduces a married woman, he is stealing property that belongs to another man. Adultery is therefore both fornication — a sin against God's moral order — and theft — a crime against another person's legally protected property. This double character is why adultery appears in this list of criminal prohibitions alongside murder and theft, while fornication does not.

The case of David and Bathsheba illustrates the point concretely. David, a mature believer and one of the greatest kings in Israel's history, simultaneously committed two crimes: he stole the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his own military officers, and then arranged Uriah's death in battle to conceal the theft. The sin was rebounded and forgiven; the crimes, however, carried consequences that extended across the remaining seventeen years of David's life. The principle embedded in David's experience is this: God forgives sin upon rebound (1 John 1:9), but crime falls under the jurisdiction of divine establishment, and God will enforce that jurisdiction directly if human courts do not. There is a supreme court in heaven, and no one escapes its docket.

Bathsheba herself, it should be noted, became the great-great-great-grandmother of the Lord Jesus Christ — a demonstration that God converts the consequences of human criminal activity into the service of His own redemptive purpose, transforming cursing into blessing.

III. Thou Shalt Not Murder

The second commandment cited is frequently mistranslated. The Greek verb is φονεύω (phoneuō), future active indicative with the negative ού (ou). This verb does not mean to kill; it means specifically to murder — to take human life unlawfully and with malice aforethought. The correct translation of the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13) is therefore “thou shalt not murder,” not “thou shalt not kill.” The distinction is legally and theologically critical.

The Word of God authorizes killing under two conditions: capital punishment as the due process of law (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:30–31), and combat on the battlefield in defense of human freedom (1 Chronicles 5:22; Isaiah 37:36). A soldier who kills the enemy in legitimate warfare is functioning honorably within the laws of divine establishment. A person who kills an attacker in lawful self-defense is likewise not committing murder. What is prohibited is the unlawful taking of human life with premeditated intent — what legal tradition defines as malice aforethought. Matthew 26:52 is typically rendered in the King James Version as 'he who lives by the sword shall die by the sword,' but the correct translation is: 'the one who has taken up the sword' — identifying a criminal, not a soldier — 'by the sword shall be executed.' This is a reference to capital punishment, not to some general principle of poetic justice.

The Origin of Murder

Murder did not originate within the human race. It originated among the angelic order. John 8:43–44 records our Lord's direct address to those who sought His death: 'You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning.' Satan, the ruler of this world (John 12:31), is not merely a deceiver; he is an arch-criminal whose primary instruments are violence and murder wherever the restraining authority of God permits their exercise. The existence of human government, law enforcement, and the military constitutes a divinely authorized restraint upon satanic criminality operating through the human race.

The first murder in human history is recorded in Genesis 4. First John 3:12 provides the interpretive key: 'not as Cain, who was of the evil one.' Cain was motivated by Satan. The background is arrogance and jealousy: Cain's grain offering was rejected by God because it was not a blood sacrifice and did not reflect faith in a coming redeemer; Abel's blood sacrifice was accepted because it did. Cain's arrogance — the assumption that his offering should have been acceptable — combined with jealousy of his brother's vindicated standing before God to produce the premeditated act of murder. Jude 10–11 describes such reversionists as those who 'have gone the way of Cain' — people whose criminal thinking is characterized by the rejection of authority, distorted perception of reality, and corruption through evil.

Proverbs 6:16–19 lists seven things that are an abomination to God: arrogance, a maligning tongue, hands that shed innocent blood (murder), a mind that devises evil schemes (conspiracy), feet that rush toward evil (rejection of authority), a false witness who utters lies (perjury), and one who spreads strife among brethren. Murder appears at the center of this catalog, and the items surrounding it — arrogance, malice, conspiracy — identify the mental attitude sins that precede and motivate the overt act. Evil is the premeditated thought; murder is the action that emerges from it.

Romans 1:29 includes murder in a cluster of interrelated sins: jealousy, murder, strife, deceit, and slander. These are described as kissing cousins. The believer who harbors jealousy and malice toward another person has the motivational foundation of murder already in place. Verbal sins — slander, gossip, maligning — constitute a form of character assassination that the passage will connect in the chapters ahead to the same category of prohibited conduct.

Murder, Crime, and Establishment Principles

Seven principles organize the treatment of murder in this verse:

1. The sixth commandment embodies the establishment principle of live and let live. As long as God permits a person to live, that person's freedom must not be abridged by taking his life.

2. The command is not 'thou shalt not kill' but 'thou shalt not murder.' Killing is authorized under specific conditions; murder is not.

3. The prohibition protects human freedom under the laws of divine establishment and simultaneously functions as a component of the royal family honor code.

4. Christian integrity includes establishment morality; the believer is not antinomian. Antinomianism is not grace function but a distortion produced by reversionism.

5. Morality is not the Christian way of life as such, but morality is necessarily included within it as part of the honor code.

6. Murder is the one crime for which Scripture explicitly mandates capital punishment (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:30–31). No ransom may substitute for the death penalty in a case of premeditated murder.

7. The prohibition of murder also prohibits verbal murder — character assassination through maligning, judging, and gossip. To destroy a person's reputation through falsehood is to commit murder against his character and his freedom to live without the intrusion of another's malice.

IV. Thou Shalt Not Steal

The eighth commandment (Exodus 20:15) appears next. The Greek verb is κλέπτω (kleptō), future active indicative with the negative ού (ou). This commandment addresses inanimate property — distinguishing it from the adultery commandment, which addressed animate property (a man's wife). Inanimate property includes land and buildings, furnishings, clothing, tools, money, and any other object that can be owned and possessed.

The commandment establishes that human freedom includes the right to own and possess property, and that this right must remain inviolate under the laws of divine establishment. It also establishes the corresponding obligation of government: government at every level exists not to solve social problems or redistribute wealth, but to protect the life, freedom, property, and privacy of every individual constituent equally. Equality before the law means that the law protects every person's freedom, privacy, and property with equal force — not that people are equal in wealth, ability, health, or any other dimension of human life.

When government expands beyond this mandate, it begins to experiment with its own citizens — imposing social programs, redistributing property, and regulating private life in ways the Constitution was designed to prevent. This is a departure from the divine purpose of government as articulated in Romans 13:1–7 and Exodus 20:15.

V. Thou Shalt Not Bear False Witness

The ninth commandment (Exodus 20:16) is next cited. The Greek is ψευδομαρτυρέω (pseudomartureō) — a compound of ψευδής (pseudēs, false) and μαρτυρέω (martureō, to give testimony in court). The correct translation is: 'you shall not commit perjury' or 'you shall not give false testimony in a legal proceeding.'

The laws of evidence require truth for jurisprudence to function. Hearsay — the admission of unverified report as though it were fact — destroys the protective function of the legal system. Scripture requires the testimony of at least two witnesses for an indictment (Numbers 35:30; Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). A single unverified accusation is insufficient. When a person lies about another person in a legal setting, he destroys that person's freedom, privacy, and reputation — committing through words the same assault upon freedom that theft commits against property and murder commits against life.

Perjury in the courtroom and slander in social life are two forms of the same underlying evil: the use of false speech to harm another person. Both are prohibited by this commandment in its broader application. The connection to the verbal sin categories of Romans 1:29–30 — slander, maligning, gossip — is direct. These are not merely moral failures; they are assaults upon the privacy and freedom of the persons targeted.

VI. Thou Shalt Not Covet

The tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17) is the final one cited in verse 9. The Greek verb is ἐπιθυμέω (epithumeō), future active indicative with the negative ού (ou), and it should be translated 'you shall not lust' or 'you shall not covet.' This is not the language of casual desire but of the consuming lust pattern of the old sin nature — the craving to possess what belongs to another.

The tenth commandment differs structurally from the preceding four in that it addresses not an overt act but a mental attitude. It prohibits the internal motivation — the covetous lust — that generates the overt crimes of adultery, murder, and theft. Coveting the life, property, persons, or possessions of another person is the seedbed from which criminal action grows. David's desire for Bathsheba is the paradigm: the lust preceded the crime, and the crime followed the lust with the predictable momentum of a stone released on a slope.

This commandment restrains the lust pattern of the old sin nature so that freedom can function under the laws of divine establishment. By addressing motivation as well as action, the Decalogue reaches into the interior life of the individual and demands not merely behavioral compliance but the orientation of the will. This is precisely the point at which the royal family honor code adds its weight to the restraint of establishment morality: the mature believer is not merely deterred from crime by fear of punishment but is internally restrained by Bible doctrine resident in the soul and by the character of the God he serves.

VII. The Summary Clause: Love as the Fulfillment of Law

Having cited five commandments from the Decalogue, Paul concludes with the summary principle already stated in verse 8: all these commandments 'are summed up in this word, namely, you shall love the other believer as yourself.' The verb is ἀνακεφαλαιόω (anakephalioō), meaning to gather up under one head, to summarize. The Decalogue's criminal prohibitions are not arbitrary; they are the legal expression of a single underlying principle. Impersonal love — the love that respects the freedom, privacy, and property of the other person without regard to personal feeling — is the category of love that fulfills the law in this context. It is not personal attraction, romantic attachment, or friendship that is in view, but the principled orientation of the will toward the well-being and freedom of the neighbor.

The four categories of love distinguished in Scripture clarify the term. Category one is personal love for God, in which the object — the Lord Jesus Christ — is the emphasis. Category two is personal love between a man and a woman, where again the object is emphasized. Category three is the friendship dimension of love among people generally. Category four — the category operative in verses 8–9 — is impersonal love, in which the emphasis falls not on the object but on the character of the person doing the loving. Impersonal love does not depend on the lovability of the neighbor; it depends on the spiritual integrity of the believer. This is the love that fulfills the law because it refuses to invade the privacy, steal the property, or destroy the life of another — not because the other has earned such treatment, but because the believer's own integrity demands it.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Five

1. Every commandment cited in Romans 13:9 describes conduct that is both a sin and a crime. Sin and crime are not synonymous but they overlap: all crimes are sins, though not all sins are crimes. The criminal prohibitions of the Decalogue address the outer boundary of freedom — the point at which sin becomes an assault upon another person's legally protected life, property, or privacy.

2. Adultery is distinct from fornication in its criminal dimension. Fornication is illicit sexual activity and is classified as sin. Adultery is also sin, but it adds the element of theft — the theft of a man's wife, who constitutes his legally recognized property under the framework of biblical and ancient Near Eastern law. This is why adultery appears in a list of criminal prohibitions alongside murder and theft.

3. The sixth commandment prohibits murder, not killing. The Greek verb φονεύω (phoneuō) specifies unlawful killing with malice aforethought. Killing in battle and killing through due process of law are authorized by Scripture (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:30–31; 1 Chronicles 5:22). Murder is the one crime for which Scripture mandates capital punishment and for which no ransom is permitted.

4. Murder originated not in the human race but in the angelic order. Satan is identified in John 8:44 as 'a murderer from the beginning.' Cain was motivated by Satan (1 John 3:12). Crime, wherever it appears in human history, is directly or indirectly traceable to the arch-criminal who rules the world system and who uses violence as one of his primary instruments.

5. The believer operates under a double restraint from criminal activity. The laws of divine establishment restrain both believer and unbeliever from crime. The royal family honor code imposes an additional restraint upon the believer. Morality is not the Christian way of life as such, but it is included within it. Antinomianism is not a product of grace but of reversionism.

6. The mature believer is the last person to escape divine discipline for crime. David's case demonstrates the principle: rebound forgives the sin, but the crime falls under divine establishment jurisdiction and God will enforce that jurisdiction directly if human courts do not. The supreme court in heaven has an unblemished conviction rate. Advancing and mature believers move progressively toward zero margin for getting away with anything.

7. The tenth commandment addresses motivation, not merely action. Ἐπιθυμέω (Epithumeō) — covetousness or lust — is the mental attitude that precedes and generates overt criminal acts. By prohibiting covetousness, the Decalogue reaches into the interior life of the individual and demands the orientation of the will, not merely behavioral compliance. Doctrine resident in the soul is the ultimate restraint upon the lust pattern of the old sin nature.

8. Impersonal love is the category of love that fulfills the law in Romans 13:8–9. Impersonal love emphasizes the character of the person doing the loving, not the lovability of the object. It respects the freedom, privacy, and property of the neighbor not because the neighbor has earned such treatment but because the believer's own spiritual integrity demands it. This is the love that summarizes all the criminal prohibitions of the Decalogue.

9. Government exists to protect life, freedom, property, and privacy — not to solve social problems. The eighth commandment's protection of property implies a corresponding governmental obligation: to defend each person's legally recognized rights with equal force. Equality before the law means equal protection of freedom, not equality of outcome or wealth. When government exceeds this mandate, it becomes an instrument of the very coercive power it was established to restrain.

10. Verbal sins — slander, gossip, maligning — constitute a form of character assassination. The prohibition of false witness extends beyond the courtroom to all false speech directed against another person. To destroy a person's reputation through fabrication is to commit verbal murder and to violate his privacy and freedom. The connection between these verbal sins and the criminal prohibitions of verse 9 will be developed further in the chapter ahead.

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
moicheuō μοιχεύω moicheuō — to commit adultery Future active indicative with the negative ou. To commit adultery — defined in this passage as theft of a married woman who constitutes her husband's legally recognized property. Distinguished from porneia (fornication) in that adultery carries the additional dimension of criminal theft.
porneia πορνεία porneia — fornication, illicit sexual activity General term for illicit sexual conduct. Classified as sin. Distinguished from adultery in that fornication does not involve the theft of another man's wife and therefore does not carry the additional dimension of crime that adultery does.
phoneuō φονεύω phoneuō — to murder Future active indicative with the negative ou. To murder — to take human life unlawfully and with malice aforethought. Distinguished from killing in battle or through capital punishment, both of which are authorized by Scripture. The correct translation of the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13).
kleptō κλέπτω kleptō — to steal Future active indicative with the negative ou. The eighth commandment (Exodus 20:15). Addresses the theft of inanimate property — any object that can be legally owned and possessed. Distinguishes from moicheuō, which addresses animate property (a man's wife).
pseudomartureō ψευδομαρτυρέω pseudomartureō — to give false testimony Compound verb: pseudēs (false) + martureō (to give testimony in court). The ninth commandment (Exodus 20:16). Prohibits perjury in legal proceedings and, by extension, all false speech directed against another person. The destruction of another's reputation through falsehood constitutes an assault upon his privacy and freedom.
epithumeō ἐπιθυμέω epithumeō — to covet, to lust Future active indicative with the negative ou. The tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17). Addresses the lust pattern of the old sin nature — the consuming desire to possess what belongs to another. Unique among the commandments cited in that it targets the mental attitude motivation that precedes and generates overt criminal acts.
anakephalioō ἀνακεφαλαιόω anakephalioō — to sum up, to gather under one head From ana (again, under) + kephalē (head). To summarize or recapitulate. Used in Romans 13:9 to describe the way in which all the criminal prohibitions of the Decalogue are gathered under the single principle of impersonal love for the neighbor.
gar γάρ gar — for, for instance Post-positive conjunctive particle. Used here in its explanatory function to link verse 9 to the principle established in verse 8. Translated 'for instance' in the corrected translation, indicating that what follows is a concrete illustration of the love-fulfills-law principle.
imperative future A Greek grammatical construction in which the future indicative with the negative ou expresses a direct command. Not a Hebraism but a construction found in classical Greek (e.g., Euripides). Used throughout the Decalogue citations in Romans 13:9 because the command necessarily involves future compliance.
malice aforethought Legal term defining the mental element required to constitute murder rather than accidental or justifiable killing. Premeditated intent to cause death or serious harm. The standard by which murder is distinguished from lawful killing in both biblical and civil law.
royal family honor code The standard of conduct expected of Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God. Includes establishment morality as a minimum and adds the additional restraint of impersonal love and personal integrity rooted in Bible doctrine. Distinct from the laws of divine establishment in that it applies to believers only.

Chapter Four Hundred Six

Romans 13:9 — The Ten Commandments, Divine Establishment, and the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 13:9 “For the commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,' and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For this: thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not commit murder, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not give false testimony, thou shalt not lust or covet — and if there be any other commandment — it is summed up in this word: you shall love your neighbor as yourself.

Romans 13:9 stands at the intersection of two great principles: the laws of divine establishment, which define and protect human freedom, and the spiritual advance of the believer toward maturity. The verse quotes five of the Ten Commandments and then moves toward a summation in the law of love — a transition the chapter will complete in the verses that follow. This chapter examines the first half of verse 9, focusing on the commandments themselves, their relation to crime and sin, and their permanent claim upon every believer under the Royal Family Honor Code.

I. The Five Commandments and Their Relation to Freedom

The five commandments quoted in Romans 13:9 — prohibiting adultery, murder, theft, false testimony, and covetousness — are not presented here as the whole of the Mosaic law. They are cited because each one defines a specific form of criminal and sinful attack upon human freedom. Understanding why each commandment appears in this context requires distinguishing between sin and crime, and understanding both in relation to the three great categories of freedom: volition, privacy, and property.

Adultery: Crime against Animate Property

The first commandment quoted is the prohibition of adultery. In the ancient legal framework reflected in both the Mosaic code and Roman law, marriage established the wife as the animate property of her husband. Adultery, therefore, is not simply an illicit sexual act — that category belongs to fornication. Adultery is the criminal intrusion upon another man's property. It combines sin (the sexual act outside its divinely ordained boundary) with crime (the theft of what belongs to another). Fornication, by contrast, is sin without the criminal dimension of property violation.

This distinction matters exegetically because verse 9 is a passage about crime as an attack upon human freedom, not merely a list of moral prohibitions. Adultery appears first because it is the paradigm case of animate property violation — the seizure of what belongs to another person by means of seduction rather than force.

Murder: Crime against Volition, Privacy, and Property Simultaneously

Murder is the only overt sin among the five commandments quoted here, and it is simultaneously the most comprehensive crime. When a person is murdered, three categories of freedom are destroyed at once: volition is permanently extinguished, privacy is violated at its most fundamental level, and the victim is permanently separated from all property, including life itself. Murder thus combines all the heinous features of criminal activity into a single irreversible act.

Theft: Crime against Inanimate Property

The prohibition of theft, coming after the prohibition of adultery, completes the picture of property violation. Adultery is the theft of animate property — the seduction of another man's wife. Theft proper is the seizure of inanimate property: money, goods, shelter, whatever belongs to another. Both are violations of freedom because freedom requires property. A person cannot advance to spiritual maturity without the basic property necessary to sustain physical life — food, shelter, clothing, transportation to Bible class. Theft attacks the material base upon which the plan of God operates in the believer's life.

False Testimony: Crime against Juridical Freedom

Perjury — bearing false witness — is a crime against the entire system of establishment law. The rule of law depends upon truth as its operating medium. When false testimony is introduced into a legal proceeding, objective law is converted into subjective manipulation. The wonderful system of establishment justice is undermined from within. This commandment therefore protects not merely the individual against false accusation, but the entire juridical framework that makes human freedom possible.

Covetousness: Heading Off Criminal Thinking at Its Source

The final commandment — thou shalt not covet or lust — operates at the level of mental attitude rather than overt act. Covetousness is included here because it is the source of criminal thinking. All criminal action begins with the desire to possess what belongs to another. This commandment does not describe a crime already committed; it describes the mental attitude that produces crime. Its inclusion reveals that establishment morality addresses not only overt violations of freedom but the internal disposition that generates those violations.

II. The Plan of God and Its Encapsulation by Establishment

To understand why Romans 13:9 matters theologically, the verse must be situated within the full structure of the Plan of God as it operates across the three radicals of the believer's experience.

The X Radical: Physical Birth to Salvation

At physical birth, human life is imputed to the body. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the old sin nature — the great equalizer, because it condemns every member of the human race to spiritual death equally. Into this condition of spiritual death, the gospel is introduced as pertinent doctrine. Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ produces the first adjustment to the justice of God: salvation. The entire X radical is encapsulated by divine establishment, because evangelism is only possible in an environment of freedom. Establishment law — the police officer protecting civil order, the military defending national sovereignty — is the precondition for the hearing of the gospel.

The Y Radical: Salvation to Spiritual Maturity

At salvation, two judicial imputations occur: all sins of the world have already been imputed to Christ on the cross (judicial imputation one), and God's righteousness is imputed to the believer at the moment of faith (judicial imputation two). This produces the second potential: blessing in time as the means of glorifying God. The second hope — absolute confidence that maturity is attained only through doctrine perceived — drives the believer forward toward the maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Maximum doctrine resident in the soul constitutes that adjustment. The Y radical is likewise encapsulated by establishment. Criminal activity is an enemy of spiritual advance because it attacks the freedom, privacy, and property that are necessary conditions for the intake of doctrine.

The Z Radical: Maturity to Eternity

At maturity, the sixth imputation — blessing in time — begins. This is replaced at the Rapture by the third hope: absolute confidence that in a resurrection body, at the judgment seat of Christ, the believer will receive the seventh imputation, great blessing and reward forever. This is the ultimate means of glorifying God. The Z radical, like the others, is sustained by the establishment framework. The man who has died in battle to preserve freedom is, in a real sense, a sponsor of the believer's advance to maturity.

Crime, then, is not merely a social problem. It is a theological enemy. It attacks freedom, and freedom is the operational environment of the Plan of God. This is why Romans 13:9 appears where it does — in the middle of the apostle's instruction on the believer's relation to governing authority. The connection is direct: establishment sustains freedom; freedom enables advance; advance glorifies God.

III. The Believer, Grace, and the Laws of Divine Establishment

A serious doctrinal error arises when grace is misunderstood as releasing the believer from the moral demands of divine establishment. This error — antinomianism — distorts grace into a license for irresponsibility. Romans 13:9 corrects it directly by quoting Mosaic commandments as binding upon New Testament believers.

The clarification required here is one of rightly dividing the Word of truth. The Church Age believer is not under the ceremonial or sacrificial dimensions of the Mosaic law. Sabbath observance, dietary regulations, the judicial penalties prescribed in the law — these are not carried over into the Church Age. But the establishment morality embedded in the Ten Commandments is carried over, precisely because it belongs not to the ceremonial system but to the universal framework of human freedom that God has established for the entire human race, believer and unbeliever alike.

Grace does not produce antinomianism. Reversionism distorts grace into antinomianism. The old sin nature — operating through sin, good, and evil — attacks establishment morality from every angle. The corrective is not to abandon grace but to understand that grace includes, rather than excludes, the moral demands of establishment.

Morality and the Believer: Inclusion and Transcendence

Two truths must be held together without collapsing one into the other. First, morality is not the Christian way of life. The rich young ruler of the Gospels illustrates this: he was morally impeccable by any standard, yet he was not a believer, and therefore could not be filled with the Holy Spirit. Morality alone cannot produce spiritual advance. Second, Christianity includes morality. The believer is not less than moral — he is moral plus. The plus is the filling of the Holy Spirit, the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), and the progressive advance to spiritual maturity.

An unbeliever can keep the moral commandments of the Decalogue. A believer can keep them as well, and then exceed them through the power of the indwelling Holy Spirit and the resident doctrine of the Word. This is the structure the apostle is preparing to complete in verse 9's second half — the summation of all commandments in the principle of impersonal love, which is beyond the reach of morality alone.

The Criminal Believer: A Contradiction of Advance

It is possible for a born-again believer to engage in criminal activity. Salvation is by faith alone, and criminal conduct does not revoke regeneration. But a believer cannot simultaneously maintain a life of crime and advance to spiritual maturity. Criminal thinking, when it persists uncorrected by doctrine, leads to criminal action. Criminal action is anti-establishment, anti-freedom — and therefore anti-advance. The believer who pursues crime will not reach the maturity adjustment to the justice of God. He will reach instead the maximum divine discipline: the sin unto death. Rebound (1 John 1:9) is always available, but it requires repudiation of criminal thinking, not merely naming criminal acts.

IV. Violence, Hope, and the Stability of the Plan of God

Romans 13:9 has immediate application to the question of violence as a means of social or political change. The passage's underlying logic is clear: crime attacks freedom, and violence is a form of crime directed against the authority structures that sustain freedom. The believer who resorts to violence — whether in personal grievance or in pursuit of a corporate cause — destroys the very framework that makes advance to maturity possible.

The apostle Paul is the definitive historical illustration. Condemned by Nero on false charges of treason, facing execution, he did not advocate insurrection. He did not call upon the churches to overthrow the imperial government. He advanced to the judgment seat of Christ under the principle of dying grace, confident in the third hope. His confidence was grounded not in political leverage but in the certainty that Jesus Christ controls history.

The principle is precise: a right cause plus a wrong method equals a wrong result. A grievance may be entirely legitimate. The moment it is pursued through violence, conspiracy, or the organized destruction of another person's freedom, the cause is forfeited. Not because the grievance was false, but because the method has made the claimant an enemy of the very freedom he claims to be defending.

Hope — the second and third hopes of the Y and Z radicals — is the antidote to violence. Hope is not passive resignation; it is active concentration on true doctrine with absolute confidence about the future. The believer who has reached the maturity adjustment concentrates on the Lord's sovereign control of history rather than on the shortcuts offered by emotional pressure, mob action, or the abuse of authority. Jesus Christ controls history. No shortcut has ever worked. No shortcut ever will.

V. Supporting Documentation from the New Testament

The obligation of believers to respect and support the laws of divine establishment is not unique to Romans 13. Three additional passages confirm and reinforce it.

Matthew 22:21 — "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Caesar's claim is the claim of divine establishment: taxes, civic obligations, respect for authority. God's claim is the claim of spiritual advance: doctrine, maturity, glorification. The two are not in competition. They operate on different planes and reinforce each other.

1 Timothy 2:1–2 — "Pray on behalf of rulers and all who are in authority, in order that we may live undisturbed and tranquil lives in all godliness and integrity." The purpose of political stability is doctrinal advance. The undisturbed and tranquil life is not an end in itself; it is the ideal condition for the function of GAP and the advance to maturity.

1 Peter 2:13–14 — "Subordinate yourselves for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether to a king as one in authority or to a governor sent by him for the punishment of those who do evil and the reward of those who do good." Submission to human authority is rendered for the Lord's sake — that is, as a function of the Royal Family Honor Code, not merely as civil prudence.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Six

1. The Ten Commandments define morality in terms of the laws of divine establishment. Human morality is necessary for the function of human freedom. The five commandments quoted in Romans 13:9 each define a specific form of criminal or sinful attack upon freedom — adultery as crime against animate property, murder as the comprehensive destruction of volition and freedom, theft as crime against inanimate property, perjury as the subversion of juridical freedom, and covetousness as the mental attitude from which all criminal action originates.

2. Adultery and fornication are categorically distinct. Fornication is illicit sexual activity — sin. Adultery is the criminal violation of another man's property through the seduction of his wife. Only a man can commit adultery, and he can only commit it with a married woman. This distinction is essential for rightly dividing the Word of truth in this passage.

3. Every born-again believer remains obligated to the laws of divine establishment. Living under grace does not release the believer from establishment morality. This includes paying taxes, respecting civil authority, serving in the military when required, and observing the moral framework of the Ten Commandments. The ceremonial and sacrificial dimensions of the Mosaic law are fulfilled and not carried over; the establishment morality is universal and permanent.

4. Antinomianism is a distortion of grace produced by reversionism. Grace does not mean freedom from moral obligation. Reversionism distorts grace into antinomianism by treating the believer's freedom from the Mosaic ceremonial system as license to ignore establishment morality. The old sin nature — operating through sin, good, and evil — attacks establishment from every direction. Doctrine is the corrective.

5. Morality protects human freedom; the Ten Commandments are the Magna Carta of human freedom. Each commandment in the Decalogue defines and defends a specific dimension of human freedom. The collective function of the Ten Commandments is to establish the conditions under which volition, privacy, and property are protected — and therefore the conditions under which the Plan of God can operate in human history.

6. All believers are required by God to observe the laws of divine establishment. This requirement is not optional, culturally conditioned, or superseded by spiritual advance. It is the permanent obligation of every member of the Royal Family of God in the Church Age.

7. Christianity is not morality, but Christianity includes morality. The believer is moral plus. The plus is the filling of the Holy Spirit and maximum doctrine resident in the soul. An unbeliever can be moral. Only a believer can be filled with the Spirit. Therefore, the believer is never less than moral; he is always more — when functioning under the Royal Family Honor Code.

8. Christianity commands morality for all believers as part of the Royal Family Honor Code. The Royal Family Honor Code integrates multiple attributes into a harmonious whole — just as military excellence requires not a single outstanding quality but a combination of qualities operating without contradiction under pressure. Moral responsibility is one essential component of that code.

9. Freedom is the operational environment of the Plan of God. For evangelism and spiritual advance, freedom is required. The source of freedom is the laws of divine establishment. Crime is anti-freedom and therefore anti-Plan of God. The believer who respects establishment supports the very framework that makes his own advance to maturity possible.

10. Morality protects human freedom and provides the environment for spiritual advance. The Ten Commandments create the conditions under which the believer can rebound, be filled with the Spirit, and take in doctrine. Morality cannot provide those spiritual functions — it can only provide the freedom within which they occur.

11. Christian dynamics include morality but exceed morality. The filling of the Holy Spirit, the function of GAP, and the advance through the Y and Z radicals are beyond the reach of morality alone. The believer's calling is moral plus — the full integration of establishment responsibility with Spirit-enabled spiritual advance.

12. A believing criminal cannot advance to spiritual maturity while maintaining a life of crime. Salvation is not revoked by criminal conduct. But criminal thinking, if uncorrected by doctrine, produces criminal action that is categorically incompatible with maturity advance. The end of a sustained criminal life is the sin unto death — maximum divine discipline — not the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

13. Spiritual maturity is the next objective after salvation, and it is always advanced through doctrine, never through violence. The mechanics of advance are the filling of the Holy Spirit and the daily function of GAP. Violence, conspiracy, and any organized attack upon establishment authority destroy the freedom necessary for advance. A right cause pursued by wrong methods becomes a wrong result. Jesus Christ controls history; there is no shortcut to anything in the Plan of God.

14. Hope is active confidence grounded in doctrine, not passive waiting or emotional pressure. Each of the three hopes — salvation hope, maturity hope, resurrection hope — is a concentration on true doctrine with absolute assurance about the future. Hope looks to the Lord for the fulfillment of His promises. The moment a believer substitutes emotional pressure, mob action, or violence for hope, he abandons the confidence that is his Royal Family inheritance and substitutes a method that destroys the very freedom on which advance depends.

15. The believer is honor bound to support establishment while advancing to maturity. This is not political preference; it is theological obligation. The police officer and the soldier are not incidental figures — they are the human instruments by which God sustains the freedom that sponsors Bible class, evangelism, and the entire operation of the Plan of God on earth.

The distinction is exegetically essential for understanding the criminal dimension of the commandments quoted in Romans 13:9.

Chapter Four Hundred Seven

Romans 13:9 — Impersonal Love as the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 13:9 “For the commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,' and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For instance this: thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not commit murder, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not give false testimony in a courtroom, thou shalt not lust — and if there is any other commandment, it is epitomized in this principle, namely, you shall love your neighbor as yourself.

Romans 13 has established the believer's obligations to governing authority, to taxation, and to the mutual debts of civil life. Verse 9 now gathers the specific negative commandments of the second table of the Decalogue — adultery, murder, theft, perjury, and covetousness — and compresses them into a single positive principle. That principle is impersonal love, the cornerstone of the Royal Family Honor Code. This chapter examines the grammar of verse 9, distinguishes impersonal from personal love, and draws out the practical implications for the believer's conduct toward other members of the human race.

I. The Five Negative Commandments as Laws of Divine Establishment

The five commandments cited in Romans 13:9 — prohibition of adultery, murder, theft, false testimony, and covetousness — are not arbitrarily selected. Each addresses a specific dimension of human freedom and the protection of property, life, reputation, and personal integrity. They function as laws of divine establishment applicable to the entire human race, believer and unbeliever alike. The unbeliever is bound by the negatives alone; the believer is bound by the negatives and additionally called to the positive principle that comprehends them all.

Every crime is simultaneously a sin, but not every sin rises to the level of crime. Crime is distinguished by its direct assault on human freedom: theft violates property; murder violates life; adultery violates the integrity of the marriage covenant; perjury subverts the administration of justice; covetousness is the motivational root from which criminal acts spring. The criminal mentality is restrained only by the coercive power of the state. The non-criminal mentality, shaped by positive volition toward doctrine, internalizes a standard that renders the external constraint secondary.

II. The Grammar of the Positive Command: Anakephalaioō

The connective conjunction καί (kai) introduces a first-class conditional clause — if, and it is true — affirming that a positive commandment exists to cover the five negatives. The verb translated 'summed up' or 'epitomized' is the present passive indicative of

the compound verb anakephalaioō (ἀνακεφαλαιόω), from ana (up, again) + kephalē (κεφαλή, head). The compound means to bring several things together under one head — to reduce to a single heading, to summarize, to epitomize. The eristic present tense marks punctiliar action in present time: the five negative commandments are now, at this point in the argument, gathered under a single positive principle. The passive voice indicates that this positive commandment — the part of the Royal Family Honor Code that applies here — receives the action: it is the instrument by which all the negatives are subsumed. The indicative mood is potential, signaling an obligation that the believer may or may not be meeting.

The prepositional phrase that follows requires precise translation. The preposition

en (ἐν) plus the locative of the demonstrative houtos (οὗτος) plus logos (λόγος) yields not 'in this saying' but 'in this principle.' The word logos here carries doctrinal weight — a governing principle, not merely a quoted saying.

The main verb of the commandment itself is the future active indicative of

agapaō (ἀγαπάω). The future tense functions as an imperative future — it expresses a command that involves ongoing future conduct. The active voice: the believer as a member of the Royal Family, functioning within the Honor Code, produces the action. The cohortative indicative with the future tense conveys the force of a binding command: thou shalt love.

The direct object is the accusative singular of

plēsion (πλησίον), an adjective used as a substantive meaning 'the one near you' — not a geographical neighbor in the modern sense, but any person in proximity: the person beside you, the colleague at work, the fellow believer in the congregation. The comparative particle hōs (ὡς) introduces the comparative clause, and the reflexive pronoun seauton (σεαυτόν), accusative singular second person, completes it: 'as yourself.' The force is not narcissistic self-regard but the internalized standards of the soul functioning as the measure of conduct toward others.

III. Personal Love and Impersonal Love: The Fundamental Distinction

The command to love the neighbor 'as yourself' directs attention to the subject rather than the object. This is the defining characteristic of impersonal love and distinguishes it absolutely from all three categories of personal love.

A. Personal Love: Object-Directed

Personal love is always directed toward a specific object. Three categories apply to the believer:

Category One: Love toward God — specifically, occupation with the person of Jesus Christ. The object is a member of the Trinity; the Father, Son, and Spirit are the exclusive objects of this category, with the Son as the manifest person of the Godhead.

Category Two: Love toward the right man or right woman — the exclusive object of romantic love within the divine design for marriage.

Category Three: Friendship love — directed toward a limited circle of personal friends, male or female, in whom there is a genuine coalescence of norms and standards at the level of the conscience.

In each personal category, the standards of the subject are associated with and projected toward the object. The quality of the love is conditioned by both the character of the subject and the attributes of the object.

B. Impersonal Love: Subject-Directed

Impersonal love has no specific object. It emphasizes the inner character and norms of the subject, not the qualities of anyone else. The standard operative in impersonal love is entirely within the believer: the norms and standards resident in the conscience as the product of Bible doctrine. Because the standard is internal, the behavior it produces is consistent regardless of who the neighbor is — attractive or repellent, agreeable or antagonistic, admirable or contemptible.

This is why the commandment reads 'as yourself': the believer does not love the neighbor on the basis of what the neighbor deserves or offers, but on the basis of what the believer himself possesses by way of doctrine-formed standards. Those standards include respect for the privacy, freedom, and property of every other person in the human race — the same freedoms protected negatively by the five commandments of the Decalogue.

Impersonal love toward the neighbor therefore means: granting the neighbor his privacy, his freedom to respond or to react, his right not to be maligned, not to be gossiped about, not to be the object of vindictive criticism or conspiratorial action. It is not affection; it is not cordiality; it is not sociability. It is the maintenance of one's own doctrinal standards in every interaction regardless of provocation.

C. The Weak Believer and the Failure of Standards

The failure of impersonal love is diagnostic of spiritual weakness. The believer who lacks doctrine-formed standards in the conscience will inevitably revert to the patterns of the old sin nature: maligning, judging, gossiping, vindictive criticism, and cowardly conspiracy. These behaviors are not accidental; they are the characteristic actions of the weak believer who attempts to draw strength by diminishing others.

Weakness in the believer takes a specific form: it seeks to neutralize the strong by attacking them — through gossip, through conspiracy formed in private, through the cultivation of coalitions against an individual who is never confronted directly. This pattern is the antithesis of impersonal love and of the Royal Family Honor Code. It violates the privacy principle, the freedom principle, and the integrity of the local assembly.

The strong believer's response is not retaliation but the maintenance of standards. To lower oneself to the level of a maligner is to become weak. To keep the mouth shut, to refuse to return gossip for gossip or conspiracy for conspiracy, is the expression of strength — the strength of doctrine resident in the soul operating through the conscience.

IV. Reciprocal and Universal Dimensions of Impersonal Love

Impersonal love, because it is standard-based rather than object-based, contains an inherent reciprocal quality. When two believers both operate from doctrine-formed standards, the result is a mutual environment of tolerance and respect that approximates the best conditions available in the devil's world prior to the Millennium. The closer the assembly of believers approximates a community of mature impersonal love, the closer it comes to the perfect environment that cannot be achieved by any social, political, or governmental program.

Impersonal love is commanded for all believers toward all other believers. It is not optional and it is not restricted to those one finds agreeable. The command includes the believer with whom one has nothing in common, the one whose standards are immature or erroneous in non-essential matters, the one whose personality is irritating or whose habits are unpleasant. Doctrine — not the corrective interference of another believer — is the proper agent for changing the erroneous standards of a fellow member of the Royal Family. The privacy of the priesthood means that each believer stands before God individually; no other believer has the authority to impose doctrinal correction except where legitimate authority structures exist (parental, marital, institutional).

V. The Doctrinal Basis: Standards in the Conscience

The capacity for impersonal love is directly proportional to the degree of Bible doctrine resident in the soul. Norms and standards formed from background, environment, or emotional experience rather than from doctrine cannot sustain impersonal love across the full range of persons the believer encounters. Background-formed standards are parochial and comparative; they generate tolerance only for those who share the same background. Doctrine-formed standards are universal in their application because they derive from the character of God, not from the accidents of human culture.

The maturity barrier is the threshold at which the believer has accumulated sufficient doctrine to operate with consistent impersonal love. Before cracking the maturity barrier, the believer lives largely on the five negative commandments as a protective framework — the 'thou shalt nots' that preserve him from catastrophic decisions while his doctrinal standards are still forming. After cracking the maturity barrier, the positive principle fully operative: the standard is now internal and self-sustaining.

This also clarifies the relationship between impersonal and personal love. Impersonal love is not a lesser form of love but the foundation of all capacity for personal love. The standards operative in impersonal love are the same standards intensified and focused in personal love. A believer who lacks adequate doctrinal standards cannot properly evaluate the objects of personal love — whether a potential friend or a potential spouse — because the measuring instrument is defective. The sequence must be: standards first, then the personal relationships that the standards make possible. Reversing the sequence produces wrong personal choices and eventual relational collapse.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seven

1. The five negative commandments of Romans 13:9 are laws of divine establishment applicable to the entire human race. They protect human freedom in its essential dimensions: life, property, sexual integrity, reputation, and motivational orientation. The unbeliever is bound by these negatives alone; the believer is additionally called to the positive principle that subsumes them.

2. The verb anakephalaioō (ἀνακεφαλαιόω) means to bring several things under one head — to epitomize. The five negative commandments are not abolished but gathered into the single positive principle of impersonal love operating within the Royal Family Honor Code.

3. Impersonal love is subject-directed, not object-directed. It emphasizes the inner character of the believer — the norms and standards resident in the conscience as a result of Bible doctrine intake — rather than the qualities or behavior of the neighbor. The command 'as yourself' points to this internal standard, not to self-love as a psychological category.

4. Impersonal love means granting the neighbor privacy, freedom, and property. It is the positive fulfillment of what the five negative commandments protect: the neighbor's right not to be violated in life, property, sexual integrity, reputation, or inner motivation. Loving the neighbor in this sense requires no affection; it requires doctrinal standards consistently maintained.

5. Personal love and impersonal love are categorically distinct. Personal love (categories one, two, and three) is always directed toward a specific object and is necessarily limited in scope. Impersonal love applies universally to all members of the human race and is commanded of every believer toward every other member of the Royal Family.

6. Gossip, maligning, vindictive criticism, and conspiracy are diagnostic of the weak believer. They represent the attempt to draw strength by diminishing others — the inversion of impersonal love. The strong believer, operating from doctrine-formed standards, does not retaliate in kind but maintains the Royal Family Honor Code regardless of provocation. Silence under attack is strength, not passivity.

7. Doctrinal standards in the conscience are the only adequate basis for impersonal love. Standards derived from background, environment, or emotional experience are parochial and will fail across the full range of human difference. Only doctrine resident in the soul — operating through the conscience — provides a universal and consistent standard that can fulfill the command to love every neighbor regardless of his characteristics.

8. Impersonal love is the foundation of personal love, not its inferior substitute. The same doctrinal standards operative in impersonal love are intensified and focused in personal love (categories one, two, and three). Acquiring standards first — through sustained doctrine intake leading to and beyond the maturity barrier — is the prerequisite for making sound decisions about personal relationships. Reversing the sequence, forming personal attachments before the standards are in place, produces wrong choices and relational instability.

9. The doctrine of the privacy of the priesthood governs the correction of immature believers. Doctrine is the proper agent for changing the erroneous non-essential standards of a fellow Royal Family member. No believer has the authority to impose doctrinal correction on another outside of legitimate authority structures (parental, marital, institutional). Impersonal love tolerates the immature believer's errors in non-essential matters and trusts doctrine and the ministry of God the Holy Spirit to produce the necessary change.

10. The community of mature believers practicing impersonal love is the closest approximation to perfect environment available in the present age. It cannot be achieved by any social program, governmental benevolence, or institutional arrangement. It is the exclusive product of Bible doctrine resident in the souls of individual believers who have cracked the maturity barrier and are advancing toward supergrace. This is the positive content of the Royal Family Honor Code as it will be developed in Romans 14.

Chapter Four Hundred Eight

Romans 13:9 — The Eleventh Commandment: Love Your Neighbor as Yourself

Romans 13:9 “For the commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,' and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For instance this: Thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not commit murder; thou shalt not steal; thou shalt not give false testimony in court; thou shalt not lust. And if there is any other commandment — and there is — it is epitomized in this principle: you shall love your neighbor as yourself.

Romans 13:9 concludes its enumeration of five commandments from the Mosaic law and then introduces the eleventh commandment of Leviticus 19:18 as the summary principle that fulfills all of them. This chapter examines the theological content of that summary commandment — its Old Testament context, its New Testament application, and its place within the royal family honor code — together with the distinction between personal and impersonal love and their relationship to spiritual maturity.

I. The Five Commandments as the Foundation of Human Freedom

The five commandments cited in Romans 13:9 are not selected arbitrarily. They define the perimeter within which human freedom operates. Freedom cannot be separated from either privacy or property, and these commandments protect both.

Thou shalt not commit adultery is the theft of animate property — the violation of a covenant relationship that belongs to another person. It is a crime against freedom in contrast to fornication, which is a sin but not in the same criminal category.

Thou shalt not commit murder is the direct termination of another person's freedom. It ends all capacity for volition until God removes that individual through natural means.

Thou shalt not steal addresses inanimate property. Property and freedom are inseparable; an attack on property is an attack on the freedom to use it.

Thou shalt not give false testimony in a court of law attacks the objective jurisprudence that freedom requires. Perjury is the functional equivalent of hearsay — it is not evidence. The principle that a person is innocent until proved guilty by the laws of evidence collapses the moment lying is introduced as testimony.

Thou shalt not lust is the intrusion upon another person's privacy through covetous desire. The inner life of another individual is not available for appropriation, and the commandment against coveting establishes that boundary at the level of thought.

These five commandments are the encapsulation of the laws of divine establishment as they define the criminal boundary. Both believers and unbelievers are required to observe them. They constitute the minimum condition for a functioning free society. Yet an unbeliever can satisfy all five and still fall short of the standard God requires of the believer — which is why the eleventh commandment is necessary.

II. The Eleventh Commandment: Leviticus 19:18 in Context

Leviticus 19:18 reads: You shall not take revenge, nor shall you bear any grudge against the sons of your people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Jehovah. This verse is the eleventh commandment — the one that fulfills the ten.

The verse is quoted throughout the New Testament, each citation confirming that the principle applies with equal force to Church Age believers as it did to Israel under Moses: Matthew 5:43; Matthew 22:39; Mark 12:31; Luke 10:27; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8. The repetition signals that loving one's neighbor is not a distinctively Mosaic obligation but a permanent expression of the divine standard.

A. The Prohibition of Revenge

The commandment opens with a negative: you shall not take revenge. Revenge is the act of lowering oneself to the standard of the person who has committed the wrong. When a mature believer responds to a wrong with retaliation, he abandons the norms and standards he has built through doctrine intake and adopts the standards of the one who wronged him. The result is a spiritual descent — the believer becomes no better than the individual who acted against him.

This is why Scripture consistently places the execution of justice in the hands of God rather than the individual. The mature believer places a wrong in the higher court — the justice of God — and leaves it there. The capacity to do so is not stoicism or indifference but a function of doctrinal norms established in the soul through years of Bible doctrine intake.

B. The Prohibition of Grudges

The second negative is the prohibition of bearing a grudge. A grudge is distinguished from overt retaliation: it is anticipated revenge — the mental attitude of retaliation without yet the opportunity. The person carrying a grudge has not yet struck back, but he has purchased a seat and is waiting for the moment.

A grudge produces the same spiritual consequence as overt revenge. The believer who carries it has already lowered his standards to those of the individual who wronged him. The cowardice of the grudge is in fact compounded: rather than confronting the issue, the aggrieved person waits, accumulates allies of similar sentiment, and eventually attacks as a group — which is both a departure from courage and from the royal family honor code.

From a practical standpoint, carrying a grudge blocks all advance toward spiritual maturity. Extended exposure to Bible doctrine will not produce growth in a soul oriented around a grudge. The soul operating under a grudge cannot achieve the objectivity required for the perception of doctrine. Life is too brief to forfeit maturity and its attendant temporal blessings and eternal rewards for the sake of a vindictive orientation toward another person.

C. The Positive Command: Impersonal Love

The contrast is introduced by the Hebrew conjunction

waw (וָ), rendered as but: but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. The conjunction is adversative — it sets the positive imperative in deliberate contrast to the two prohibitions that precede it.

The phrase 'as yourself' does not require the believer to possess self-love as an emotional quantity and then replicate that emotion toward the neighbor. That reading produces narcissism and emotional confusion. The correct interpretation is that the believer loves the neighbor on the basis of his own developed norms and standards. The emphasis is on the subject — the believing lover — not on the object. This is the definition of impersonal love.

III. Personal Love and Impersonal Love Distinguished

Two categories of love operate in the Christian life and they must be distinguished clearly.

A. Personal Love

In personal love the emphasis falls on the object. The object is what attracts, what sustains, what gives the relationship its quality. Personal love operates in three categories:

Category 1: Personal love for the Lord Jesus Christ. This is the primary category and the foundation of all other love. It is built from doctrinal content in the soul — frame of reference, memory center, categorical storage, conscience — and is the precondition for all genuine impersonal love.

Category 2: Personal love between right man and right woman. The soul enters into love here, not merely the body. Standards attract standards; the principle that opposites attract is a popular misconception. Like attracts like, and the doctrinal norms formed in the soul are what draw people of compatible standards together.

Category 3: Personal love between friends. The closest friendships are those in which the mutual standards of the soul — including relaxed mental attitude, non-retaliation, refusal to malign, and freedom from vindictive orientation — are shared.

B. Impersonal Love

In impersonal love the emphasis falls on the subject — the believer who loves. The object is not what drives the love. The believer loves every member of the human race, specifically the brethren, not because they are attractive or admirable but because his own developed norms and standards are high enough to sustain that posture regardless of the behavior of others.

Impersonal love is the mechanism by which the believer avoids retaliation, avoids gossip, avoids maligning, avoids vindictive criticism, and grants other believers the privacy of their priesthood. It tolerates false norms in the weak believer because it recognizes that doctrine — not spiritual pressure from a legalist — is the only legitimate corrective of incorrect norms and standards.

The movement from impersonal to personal is possible and normal. A believer begins with impersonal love toward everyone in the congregation and over time, as certain individuals demonstrate compatible standards, some of those individuals are transferred to the personal category as genuine friends. But not everyone makes that transfer, and forcing it — smothering the other person with personal attention, invading their privacy, attacking their freedom to maintain other friendships — destroys the very basis of the relationship. Impersonal love includes the freedom of the other person to exist on their own terms.

C. The Danger of Smothering

Personal love, when it becomes possessive, destroys itself. The volition and privacy of the other person are essential to the continuation of the relationship. A man who stifles a woman's freedom destroys her capacity to respond. A woman who treats a man as her exclusive property destroys his. Privacy is not an optional feature of relationship; it is the condition that makes genuine response possible. Love that smothers is not love — it is control, and it destroys what it claims to prize.

IV. The Eleventh Commandment in the New Testament

A. Mark 12:28–31

A scribe — a student of the Old Testament canon — heard Jesus answer the legalists well and asked him directly: What commandment is first of all? Jesus responded with the Shema: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord. Then: you shall love the Lord your God with all of your right lobe, with all of your soul, with all of your mental attitude, with all of your strength.

The correct translation renders the Greek term commonly translated 'heart' as the right lobe of the soul — the area of doctrinal storage, categorical thinking, and conscience. This is not sentimental or emotional love; it is love built from the entire content of the soul as organized by Bible doctrine. From this personal love for the Lord, secondary impersonal love for the neighbor becomes possible: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.

The logical sequence is important: personal love for the Lord generates the doctrinal standards in the soul that qualify the believer for impersonal love toward others. You cannot sustain impersonal love without the personal love that creates the standards to maintain it.

B. Galatians 5:14

Galatians 5:14 states: For the entire law is fulfilled in one principle according to the scripture — you shall love your neighbor as yourself. The Greek term translated fulfilled is peplērōtai (πεπλήρωται), perfect passive indicative of plēroō (πληρόω): to fill up to the full measure, to bring to complete expression. Impersonal love does not abolish the law; it fulfills it by embodying its entire intent in a single operational principle.

C. James 2:8

James 2:8 identifies this commandment explicitly as the royal law: If however you are fulfilling the royal law according to the scripture — you shall love your neighbor as yourself — in this you are doing well. The designation 'royal law' connects the commandment to the royal family of God and to the royal family honor code. It is not simply the law of Moses carried forward unchanged; it is that law now operating within the framework of the Church Age believer's identity as a member of the royal family.

V. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Eleventh Commandment

The eleventh commandment as quoted in Romans 13:9 and reinforced throughout the New Testament is not merely a moral exhortation — it is the summary expression of the royal family honor code in its relational dimension. The honor code has two axes: the believer's relationship with God (personal love, doctrine intake, filling of the Spirit) and the believer's relationship with other members of the human race (impersonal love, non-retaliation, privacy, toleration of the weak believer).

The first half of Romans 13:9 addresses morality — the obligation to observe the laws of divine establishment that protect freedom. This applies to the entire human race. The second half addresses integrity — the additional standard demanded of the believer through the filling of the Spirit and maximum doctrine intake. Morality can be attained by the unbeliever; integrity in the sense described here is available only to the believer functioning in the royal family honor code.

The rich young ruler is the paradigm case of morality without integrity. He kept the ten commandments perfectly and maintained a careful record of his compliance. But the record became the foundation for the largest accumulation of arrogance and self-righteousness imaginable, and it left him without the capacity for impersonal love. He was not a criminal. But he was not a lover either. He occupied the space between the two without the doctrine that would have moved him past the morality barrier into genuine integrity.

The weak believer is full of false norms and goofy opinions. The mature believer tolerates these on all non-essential matters because toleration is the operational expression of impersonal love. Only when the weak believer encroaches on an essential — denying the deity of Christ, repudiating salvation by faith alone, rejecting a critical doctrine — does separation become appropriate. On non-essentials, the privacy of the weak believer's priesthood is inviolable. Bible doctrine, not spiritual pressure from a stronger believer, is the only legitimate instrument for correcting false norms.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eight

1. The five commandments of Romans 13:9 define the criminal boundary of human freedom. They protect animate property (adultery), life (murder), inanimate property (theft), objective jurisprudence (false testimony), and privacy (coveting). Both believers and unbelievers are obligated to observe them.

2. The eleventh commandment of Leviticus 19:18 fulfills the ten. It does so not by adding a new content but by supplying the positive principle — impersonal love — that the ten commandments, taken negatively, cannot themselves generate.

3. Revenge is self-degradation. The believer who retaliates against a wrong lowers himself to the standard of the wrongdoer. The mechanism for avoiding this is to place all wrongs in the higher court of divine justice and leave them there.

4. A grudge is anticipated revenge. It inflicts the same spiritual damage as overt retaliation — the believer descends to the standards of the person wronging him — without yet acting. Carrying a grudge blocks doctrinal objectivity and forfeits advance toward maturity.

5. Impersonal love is defined by the subject, not the object. The phrase 'as yourself' means on the basis of your developed norms and standards — not a self-referential emotion replicated toward others. The believer maintains his doctrinal standards regardless of the behavior of the person being loved.

6. Personal love for the Lord Jesus Christ is the precondition for impersonal love toward others. The doctrinal content built in the soul through category-one personal love creates the norms and standards that make sustained impersonal love possible. Without doctrine, impersonal love collapses into sentimentalism or disappears entirely.

7. Smothering destroys love. Personal love that invades the privacy or suppresses the volition of its object eliminates the very conditions that make the relationship flourish. Privacy is not a preference but a structural requirement of all genuine love relationships.

8. Toleration of the weak believer is the relational expression of impersonal love. False norms in the immature believer are corrected by doctrine alone, not by spiritual coercion. The mature believer grants the weak believer the privacy of his priesthood while continuing to grow in his own doctrinal standards.

9. The eleventh commandment is now part of the royal family honor code. Identified in James 2:8 as the royal law, it governs Church Age believers in their relational obligations — both toward the brethren and toward all members of the human race — within the framework of the Protocol Plan of God.

10. Morality and integrity are not the same. The unbeliever can fulfill the five commandments of Romans 13:9a; the rich young ruler did so perfectly. But the impersonal love of Romans 13:9b — the integrity standard of the royal family honor code — is available only to the Spirit-filled believer advancing in doctrine.
