Chapter Four Hundred Fifteen

Romans 13:11–14 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Walking Honorably

Romans 13:11–14 “Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: This do also, having known the period of time, that it is already time for you to wake up from sleep, for now our deliverance is nearer than when we believed. The night is far gone, the day is approaching. Therefore let us lay aside the works of darkness, let us put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the daytime — not in rioting and drunkenness, not in fornication and licentiousness, not in strife and jealousy.

Romans 13 draws to its close with a summary command that brings together the entire preceding argument about governing authority, love of the brethren, and the fulfillment of the Mosaic law. The command to walk honorably as in the daytime (verse 13) is the operational summary of the Royal Family Honor Code. Three paired negatives then define, from the bottom up, what dishonoring conduct looks like — social immorality, sexual immorality, and personality immorality. This chapter examines the completed review of the Royal Family Honor Code (points 3–9) and then works through the three couplets of verse 13 in detail.

I. The Royal Family Honor Code — Completed Review (Romans 13:11–13a)

Point 3 — Loving the Brethren: Personal Love and Impersonal Love

The command of verse 9 — 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — is not an invitation to sentimental attachment. The Greek idiom means: love the one near you on the basis of your own standards. This is the distinction between personal love and impersonal love, and the honor code is built on understanding both.

Personal love emphasizes the object of love. Its three legitimate categories are: (1) the Lord Jesus Christ, (2) the right woman or right man, and (3) friends, children, parents, and relatives. These categories are appropriate because the object qualifies for the highest personal attention and affection that the subject can give.

Impersonal love, by contrast, emphasizes the norms and standards of the subject — the one doing the loving. Its object is every fellow believer in one's social or professional sphere, regardless of compatibility, temperament, or personal appeal. The standards applied in impersonal love are not generated by the object but by the doctrine resident in the soul of the subject.

The phrase hōs seauton (ὡς σεαυτόν) — 'as yourself' — is not a psychological norm about self-esteem. It is a Greek idiom for 'on the basis of your own standards.' The standard is not the fluctuating opinion one holds of oneself, but the objective doctrinal norms resident in the soul through sustained perception of Bible doctrine.

The following principles govern the operation of impersonal love within the honor code:

1. This command cannot be obeyed until one understands the difference between essential and non-essential matters, and the distinction between personal and impersonal love.

2. Personal love emphasizes the object; impersonal love emphasizes the norms and standards of the subject.

3. All love — personal and impersonal — is based on standards and capacities derived from doctrine.

4. The essential difference between the two forms of love is how those standards are applied: to the object in personal love, to the subject in impersonal love.

5. Impersonal love means treating fellow believers on the basis of one's own integrity, norms, and standards — not on the basis of their behavior toward the believer.

6. Impersonal love cannot be reduced to the level of retaliatory conduct. It excludes grudges, retaliation, and revenge. To retaliate against a fellow believer is to lower oneself to the standards of the antagonist. The honor code demands that the believer remain a protagonist, not an antagonist.

7. Loving the brethren begins with the attributes of God; divine standards must govern its execution.

8. Every believer receives the righteousness of God imputed at salvation. Loving the brethren therefore means respect for the righteousness of God wherever it is found. A grudge held against a fellow believer is a failure to respect that imputed righteousness — and in that sense is itself a form of irreverence.

9. Loving the brethren is a relaxed mental attitude: freedom from mental attitude sins that generate revenge, retaliation, personality conflict, and their motivational roots — arrogance, jealousy, hatred, antagonism, bitterness, vindictiveness, and guilt.

10. In contrast to the popular distortion, the love of the brethren is not overt friendliness, effusive sociability, or performative warmth. The honor code does not require or reward these expressions. Privacy given to another believer is itself an act of love. The honor code protects the privacy of the royal priesthood; it does not abolish social distance.

11. Love is the filling of the Spirit and the application of doctrinal standards by which the honor code functions. It operates through the subject's standards rather than through reciprocal response to attention, flattery, affection, or attraction.

12. The Royal Family Honor Code functions under the filling of the Spirit and doctrine resident in the soul to produce respect for the privacy, freedom, and property of all believers, plus toleration of differences of opinion in non-essential and incidental matters.

13. The love of the brethren excludes all gossip, maligning, judging, revenge, retaliation, and grudges toward other members of the royal family of God.

Point 4 — The Common Objective: Advance to Maturity

The Royal Family Honor Code recognizes that the common objective for every believer in time is advance to the maturity adjustment to the justice of God — and that this advance is only possible through the daily intake of doctrine. This is the organizing principle of the believer's life in the Church Age.

The only means by which the objectives of glorifying God and advancing to maturity can be achieved is through the perception of Bible doctrine — not through production, not through giving, and not through self-sacrifice. What the believer is in his thinking is what he is. Doctrine resident in the soul is the substance of spiritual advance. Activity without doctrine produces neither legitimate motivation nor legitimate production.

The honor code therefore demands that each believer have the same opportunity to take in doctrine. This has immediate practical consequences for corporate behavior: unnecessary movement, conversation, or any distraction that interferes with another believer's concentration violates the honor code. Respect for the learning environment is itself an expression of impersonal love.

Point 5 — The Honor Code Builds Integrity Without Rejecting Morality

The Royal Family Honor Code does not reject morality. Morality is required of both believer and unbeliever as a function of the laws of divine establishment. The honor code, however, establishes a higher standard for the royal family — a standard of integrity that requires the filling of the Spirit and the perception of doctrine for its execution. Christianity is not merely a morality system. It does not exclude morality; it exceeds morality. When the believer fulfills the honor code, he has already met the moral standard and surpassed it.

Point 6 — The Honor Code Excludes Production as the Means of Blessing

Christian production — witnessing, prayer, giving, service in the local church — is commanded and is not wrong in itself. The error arises when any of these activities is performed with the expectation of eliciting divine blessing. When production is treated as the means of blessing, the result is legalism and its attendant discipline, including the possibility of the sin unto death. Neither legitimate activities commanded by Scripture nor self-imposed ascetic exercises can secure blessing from God.

All blessing flows from the justice of God to the believer who has advanced to maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Talent, personality, morality, asceticism, and sacrificial giving do not elicit divine blessing. The attainment of maturity through the perception of doctrine is the only means by which God is glorified and blessing is received.

A further distinction applies here. Under the royal priesthood, the believer takes in doctrine and advances to maturity. Under royal ambassadorship, the mature believer produces legitimate works as the result of doctrine and the filling of the Spirit — not as a means to anything, but as the overflow of what he has become.

Point 7 — Hope as Total Dependence on the Integrity of God

Total dependence on the integrity of God is called hope, and hope is integral to the Royal Family Honor Code. The three hopes correspond to the three stages of the divine plan as expressed in the formula X + Y + Z.

In the X bracket, human life is imputed at birth together with Adam's original sin, producing total condemnation. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel. The first hope is absolute confidence that by believing in Christ the believer receives eternal life. This hope is replaced by the reality of salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ.

In the Y bracket, the believer moves from salvation toward maturity. Two judicial imputations have occurred: all personal sins were imputed to Christ at the cross and judged, and God's righteousness was imputed to the believer at salvation. These establish the second potential: the potential for divine blessing and for glorifying God. The pertinent doctrine advances the believer to maturity. The second hope is absolute confidence that through daily perception of doctrine and the attainment of spiritual maturity the believer glorifies God and receives the imputation of divine blessing. This hope is replaced by the reality of maturity adjustment to the justice of God through the perception of Bible doctrine.

In the Z bracket, the mature believer has received the imputation of eternal life at salvation and the imputation of divine blessing at maturity. The third potential is great reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ. The pertinent doctrine at this stage is undeserved suffering, which keeps the believer's perspective oriented toward eternity rather than toward present blessing. The third hope is absolute confidence that after the Rapture, standing in a resurrection body, the believer will receive the seventh imputation — the realization of Romans 8:28 — the fulfillment of the plan of God and the glorification of God forever.

Each of the three hopes is related to the Royal Family Honor Code. Hope at salvation admits the believer into the aristocracy of the royal family. The second and third hopes are integrated into the daily function of the honor code.

Point 8 — The Honor Code and Divine Imputation

The Royal Family Honor Code is related to divine imputation at every stage, as every facet of the plan of God is related to divine imputation. The X + Y + Z formula demonstrates that imputation — judicial and real — is the structural mechanism by which God's blessing is dispensed, and the honor code is the operational context in which the believer positions himself to receive it.

Point 9 — Summary of the Royal Family Honor Code

The Royal Family Honor Code is organized around four relationships: to God, to nation, to people, and to self. It incorporates the morality of divine establishment — with its emphasis on freedom, privacy, and property — and advances that morality to a higher standard of integrity that can only be fulfilled through the filling of the Holy Spirit and the maximum intake of doctrine.

Freedom under establishment includes privacy and property and cannot be separated from them. Within the Royal Family Honor Code, these same protections are amplified: privacy is protected by the royal priesthood, and property is secured by logistical grace and the blessings of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

II. Walking Honorably: Three Couplets of Prohibition (Romans 13:13)

The command 'Let us walk honorably as in the daytime' is immediately followed by three paired negatives. Each couplet identifies a category of conduct that violates the honor code. The structure is deliberate: in each case, the second term in the couplet identifies a cause or intensifying condition for the first. All three categories are forbidden to the unbeliever under the laws of divine establishment; all three are equally forbidden to the believer under the Royal Family Honor Code. The verse thus demonstrates that the grace principle does not sponsor antinomianism.

Category 1 — Social Immorality: Rioting and Drunkenness

The first couplet pairs kōmos (κῶμος) and methē (μέθη). The subjunctive mood with the negative particle mē (μή) produces a hortatory prohibition: 'let us not.'

Kōmos originally denoted a processional celebration in honor of Dionysus. Because such processions characteristically descended into disorder, the term came to mean a riotous assembly — a group in which recognized authority has been set aside and every participant does as he pleases. Translated 'rioting' in the corrected translation, kōmos represents the rejection of externally constituted authority: civil authority, spiritual authority, the authority of the employer, the commanding officer, or the school administrator. Freedom without authority is not freedom. The honor code requires submission to every duly constituted authority — whether in the civil realm (the police officer, the judge) or in the spiritual realm (the pastor-teacher as the delegated teaching authority).

Methē is drunkenness — the rejection not of another's authority but of one's own. Where kōmos is arrogance toward external authority, methē is the failure of internal volition. God gave the believer free will in order to regulate his own life. When that volition fails to set appropriate limits — whether with respect to alcohol or any other area of self-governance — the result is the abdication of self-discipline. Drunkenness is not only a sin; it is a symptom of a broader failure to exercise volitional self-regulation. The Scripture does not prohibit the use of alcohol; it prohibits the state of drunkenness as a sin and as a mark of volitional collapse.

The two terms are related: rioting is the rejection of someone else's authority; drunkenness is the rejection of one's own. Together they define social immorality as the breakdown of all authority — external and internal.

Category 2 — Sexual Immorality: Fornication and Licentiousness

The second couplet pairs koitē (κοίτη) and aselgeia (ἀσέλγεια).

Koitē in this context means illicit sexual intercourse and should be translated 'fornication.' It encompasses both normal and abnormal forms of sexual sin. Normal fornication is sexual intercourse between an unmarried man and woman outside of marriage. Abnormal fornication covers the full spectrum of sexual degeneracy: multiple partners, homosexuality, lesbianism, bestiality, and pederasty. When sexual sin passes from the normal to the abnormal, it becomes degeneracy in the technical sense: a sin that involves the corruption of the created order and the destruction of the norms of divine establishment. Homosexual degeneracy in particular has historically been correlated with social and national collapse, as the historical examples of Athens and Weimar Germany attest.

Aselgeia is best rendered 'licentiousness' or 'wantonness.' It refers not to the act of fornication but to the mental and attitudinal orientation that lusts after illicit sexual experience without necessarily proceeding to an overt act. It is the unbridled condition of a mind that has ceased to regulate its own desires. Like methē, it represents a failure of volitional self-discipline — the failure to govern one's own thought life. This category is included precisely because many who would never commit an overt act of fornication nonetheless indulge the mental equivalent without restraint.

Self-discipline — the capacity to govern one's own soul — is itself a fruit of doctrine resident in the soul. The honor code demands both overt regulation (avoidance of fornication) and inner regulation (avoidance of licentiousness).

Category 3 — Personality Immorality: Strife and Jealousy

The third couplet pairs eris (ἔρις) and zēlos (ζῆλος).

Eris means discord or contention — the kind of strife that arises from mental attitude sins. When the believer cannot control his own thinking, arrogance, jealousy, vindictiveness, and petty antagonism express themselves in relational conflict. Eris is the overt result.

Zēlos in this negative context means jealousy — the mental attitude sin that precedes the outbreak of eris. Jealousy is the failure of self-discipline at the level of mental attitude. It causes the believer to orient toward the object of jealousy not with the impersonal love the honor code demands but with a destructive personal animosity. Jealousy seeks to diminish or destroy its object through maligning, gossip, judging, grudge-bearing, and retaliation. The mental attitude sin produces the overt result: strife.

The structure of this third couplet — jealousy producing strife — illustrates a structural principle that governs all three categories: in each couplet, overt immorality has an internal cause. Rioting originates in the rejection of external authority; drunkenness in the rejection of self-regulation; licentiousness in the ungoverned mind; and strife in jealousy as a mental attitude sin.

The Structure of the Three Categories

The three couplets are organized around three domains of immorality:

Category 1 — Social immorality (rioting and drunkenness): breakdown of authority, both external and internal.

Category 2 — Sexual immorality (fornication and licentiousness): breakdown of self-regulation in act and thought.

Category 3 — Personality immorality (strife and jealousy): breakdown of mental attitude under the influence of the old sin nature.

In each category, there is a result preceded by its cause. All three categories of immorality are forbidden to the unbeliever under the laws of divine establishment. All three are equally forbidden to the believer under the Royal Family Honor Code. The verse forms the obvious conclusion that Christianity and the principle of grace do not sponsor antinomianism. The believer's responsibility under the honor code includes the morality demanded by divine establishment, but the honor code goes far beyond morality — making demands on the believer that can only be fulfilled through the filling of the Holy Spirit and the maximum intake of doctrine.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Fifteen

1. Impersonal love is the operational mode of the Royal Family Honor Code. The command to love one's neighbor 'as yourself' is not a psychological norm about self-regard. It is a Greek idiom directing the believer to treat fellow believers on the basis of his own doctrinal norms and standards, regardless of their behavior. Personal love focuses on the object; impersonal love focuses on the subject's integrity.

2. Holding a grudge against a fellow believer is a failure to respect the righteousness of God. Every member of the royal family has received the righteousness of God as a judicial imputation at salvation. To maintain a grudge against a fellow believer is to disregard that imputed righteousness — and constitutes a form of irreverence toward the divine attribute from which it derives.

3. The honor code exceeds morality without abandoning it. Morality is required of all people under the laws of divine establishment. The believer meets the moral standard and surpasses it. The higher standard of integrity demanded by the honor code can only be executed through the filling of the Holy Spirit and the sustained intake of doctrine.

4. Christian production is not the means of divine blessing. Witnessing, prayer, giving, and service are all commanded activities. They are not, however, the mechanism by which divine blessing is secured. All blessing flows through the justice of God to the believer who has advanced to maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Production performed as a means of blessing is legalism and produces reversionism discipline.

5. Hope is total dependence on the integrity of God at each stage of the divine plan. The three hopes correspond to salvation adjustment, maturity adjustment, and the judgment seat of Christ (the seventh imputation). Each is an absolute confidence about a future fact: eternal life, the imputation of divine blessing at maturity, and eternal reward after the Rapture.

6. Rioting and drunkenness are both failures of authority. Rioting (kōmos) is the rejection of externally constituted authority; drunkenness (methē) is the failure of internal volitional self-regulation. The honor code requires submission to duly constituted authority in every sphere — civil, spiritual, familial, and professional.

7. Fornication encompasses both normal and abnormal sexual sin. The corrected translation renders koitē as 'fornication,' which includes not only normal illicit intercourse but all forms of sexual degeneracy. Licentiousness (aselgeia) addresses the ungoverned mental orientation that precedes or substitutes for the overt act. Both categories are governed by the principle of volitional self-discipline.

8. Personality immorality originates in uncontrolled mental attitude. Jealousy (zēlos) is the cause; strife (eris) is the result. Mental attitude sins — arrogance, jealousy, vindictiveness, bitterness, implacability — are the internal engine of overt relational breakdown. Impersonal love, sustained by doctrine and the filling of the Spirit, is the antidote.

9. Each couplet in verse 13 reveals that overt immorality has an internal cause. The three categories — social, sexual, personality — each present a result preceded by its generating condition. This structure underscores that the battleground of the honor code is first the soul, then overt behavior.

10. The command to walk honorably summarizes the entire operational mandate of the Royal Family Honor Code. It encompasses respect for authority, sexual self-discipline, and freedom from the mental attitude sins that produce relational strife. The positive execution of this command — walking honorably as in the daytime — requires the filling of the Holy Spirit and maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

Chapter Four Hundred Sixteen

Romans 13:14 — The Positive Command: Put On the Lord Jesus Christ

Romans 13:14 “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But put on the Lord Jesus Christ and stop making provision for your flesh, your old sin nature, because of its lusts.

Romans 13:14 is a transitional verse bridging the closing imperatives of chapter 13 to the extended treatment of the royal family honor code in chapter 14. The verse condenses in a single command the entire program of the believer's advance to maturity: put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Everything that follows in chapter 14 — the relationship between the strong believer and the weak believer — is the outworking of that command in concrete human relationships.

I. The Adversative Conjunction and Its Force

The verse opens with the strong adversative conjunction

The verse opens with the strong adversative conjunction alla (αλλά), translated 'but.' This adversative sets up a direct contrast between the negative commands of the preceding verse — the catalogue of sins belonging to the darkness: carousing, drunkenness, sexual immorality, sensuality, quarreling, and jealousy — and the single comprehensive positive command that now follows. The negative prohibitions of verse 13 are answered not by a new list of virtues but by one commanding act: put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

II. The Command: Aorist Middle Imperative of endyō

The verb rendered 'put on' is the aorist middle imperative of endyō (ενδύω), meaning to clothe oneself, to put on a garment. The form is significant at every level.

A. The Aorist: Culminative Force

The aorist here is a culminative aorist. It views the entire advance to maturity as a single whole, but emphasizes the result rather than the process. The daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception — doctrine received, metabolized, and applied day after day — is gathered into one comprehensive result: maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The aorist does not minimize the process; it focuses the believer's attention on where the process is going.

B. The Middle Voice: Direct Middle

The middle voice is a direct middle, indicating that the subject participates directly in the results of the action. The believer who puts on the Lord Jesus Christ is himself the beneficiary of that action. This is not passive reception but volitional engagement — the believer advances to maturity and directly appropriates the result.

C. The Imperative Mood: Appeal to Volition

The imperative mood makes this a command addressed to the will of the individual believer. Spiritual maturity is not automatic. It requires a volitional decision — sustained, daily, and non-negotiable — to remain under the intake of Bible doctrine. The command form indicates that God regards this advance as both possible and obligatory for every member of the royal family.

III. The Direct Object: The Lord Jesus Christ

The three direct objects in the accusative singular — Kyrion (Κύριον), Iēsoun (Ιησοῦν), Christon (Χριστόν) — together identify the full person and office of the Savior. The command is not to put on a system of doctrine in the abstract, but to put on a person: the Lord Jesus Christ. This is significant because maturity adjustment to the justice of God is inseparable from occupation with the person of Christ. Occupation with Christ is both the means and the mark of genuine spiritual maturity. This command must not be confused with the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which occurs at the moment of salvation and places the believer in union with Christ irrevocably. That is phase one, non-volitional, and unrepeatable. The command here is phase two: advance to maturity through sustained doctrine intake under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

IV. The Contrast with the Garden: Fig Leaves versus Christ

The imagery of putting on a garment carries immediate resonance with Genesis 3. When Adam and Eve were expelled from the garden, their first act was to fashion coverings from fig leaves — a self-initiated adjustment designed to resolve their sense of exposure and disorder. The adjustment was directed at each other, not at God. By manufacturing a social solution to a spiritual problem, they demonstrated the fundamental error that has characterized human history ever since: the attempt to become right with the human race rather than right with God.

Romans 13:14 is the direct counter to that impulse. The command is not to adjust horizontally — not to remake social structures, not to reform institutions, not to eliminate visible suffering from one's field of vision — but to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. The vertical relationship with God, expressed through maximum doctrine resident in the soul, is what resolves the true problem of human existence. Horizontal adjustments, however well-intentioned, are fig leaves.

V. The Negative Command: Stop Making Provision for the Old Sin Nature

The second clause employs the present middle imperative of poieō (ποιέω) — to do, to make, to produce — negated by the particle mē (μή). The combination of an imperative of prohibition with the present tense yields the force: stop doing what you are currently doing. The present tense is descriptive, indicating an ongoing activity that is to cease.

A. Pronoia: Foresight as Provision

The noun translated 'provision' is pronoia (πρόνοια), from pro (before) + nous (mind, thought). The word means foresight, forethought, and by natural extension, advance provision. Making provision for the old sin nature means directing one's mental energy — one's planning, attention, and time — toward satisfying the appetites of the old sin nature rather than toward the advance to maturity.

B. Sarx: The Old Sin Nature

The object of this negative command is sarx (σάρξ), here referring specifically to the old sin nature. The definite article functions as a possessive pronoun: 'your flesh,' 'your old sin nature.' The verse does not command the elimination of the old sin nature — sinless perfection is not attainable in phase two — but the refusal to allocate one's resources, attention, and energy to its satisfaction.

C. Epithymia: The Lusts of the Old Sin Nature

The prepositional phrase eis epithymias (εἰς ἐπιθυμίας), 'with reference to its lusts,' employs the plural of epithymia (ἐπιθυμία), meaning strong desire, craving, lust. The plural is significant: it encompasses the full range of distractions that the old sin nature can generate. These are not limited to overtly sinful appetites. The lusts of the old sin nature include the entire spectrum of pursuits — moral and immoral, socially approved and condemned — that divert the believer from the daily intake of doctrine. A crusade to reform society, a consuming ambition in business, a project that occupies the mind during the time allotted to doctrine: all of these qualify as epithymiai in the sense Paul intends. The lusts are anything that functions as foresight of the flesh — anything the old sin nature plans and pursues as an alternative to putting on the Lord Jesus Christ.

VI. The Royal Family Honor Code and Chapter 14

Romans 13:14 is simultaneously a conclusion to the governing imperatives of chapter 13 and a prologue to chapter 14. The advance to maturity commanded here — putting on the Lord Jesus Christ through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception — is precisely what equips the believer to fulfill the royal family honor code that chapter 14 will unfold in detail.

Chapter 14 addresses the relationship between the strong believer and the weak believer: two categories of genuine believers separated not by geography but by doctrine, by the depth of their adjustment to the justice of God. The strong believer, having advanced through the maturity barrier, has the capacity to bear with the scruples of the weak without either condemning them or capitulating to their standards. The weak believer, still governed by the old sin nature's system of taboos and legalistic categories, lacks that capacity. The only remedy for the weak believer is the same command given here: put on the Lord Jesus Christ. The royal family honor code cannot be manufactured by social engineering or institutional reform. It is the outgrowth of maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

The filling of the Holy Spirit is the indispensable means by which the Grace Apparatus for Perception functions. Putting on the Lord Jesus Christ therefore implicitly requires the recovery of that filling whenever it is lost — that is, rebound: the naming of known sins to God, restoring fellowship and the enabling ministry of the Spirit (1 John 1:9). Advance to maturity, rebound, and the filling of the Spirit are not separable operations; they form a single integrated modus operandi for the royal family in phase two.

VII. Christianity's Relationship to Society and Government

The exegesis of Romans 13:14 provides the foundation for a set of governing principles concerning the believer's relationship to the world order:

Christianity is adaptable to any human society under all conditions of life. It is not hostile to any specific form of government and does not sponsor or recommend any particular political arrangement. The only form of government that could be called intrinsically compatible with the divine order is an absolute monarchy — and that will obtain only in the Millennium, under the reign of the Lord Jesus Christ. All present human governments are provisional arrangements under the laws of divine establishment.

Christianity is opposed to all evil in government and society insofar as evil destroys freedom, privacy, authority, property, evangelism, and spiritual growth. But the believer's calling is not to correct evil directly. Only the Lord can correct evil in any generation. The believer is called to grow in grace, to advance to maturity, and to function as a member of the pivot — the body of mature believers whose adjustment to the justice of God sustains divine blessing on the national entity.

Christianity teaches orientation to life through respect for authority ordained by God — whether in the laws of divine establishment or in the modus operandi of the local church. A society experiencing turbulence and the breakdown of authority has every reason to welcome the stabilizing influence of a doctrinally mature community of believers. The pivot is the salt of the land. Without the free function of the local church, life in any society trends toward anarchy and dissolution.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixteen

1. Romans 13:14 is transitional. It closes the governing imperatives of chapter 13 and opens the extended treatment of the royal family honor code in chapter 14. The verse is the hinge on which the entire argument turns: the horizontal relationships of chapter 14 are only possible on the vertical foundation commanded here.

2. The aorist middle imperative of endyō is a culminative aorist. It views the entire advance to maturity in its totality but emphasizes the result. The command is not a single act at a single moment but the result of sustained daily doctrine intake gathered into one comprehensive outcome: maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

3. The command is addressed to phase two, not phase one. Union with Christ (the baptism of the Holy Spirit) occurs at salvation and requires no command. The imperative here addresses the believer in the post-salvation life, calling for a volitional, daily, sustained advance to spiritual maturity.

4. Maturity adjustment is inseparable from occupation with the person of Christ. The command specifies the Lord Jesus Christ as the object of the putting-on precisely because maturity cannot be reduced to abstract doctrinal accumulation. The content of doctrine is the person and work of Christ, and maturity is characterized by occupation with him.

5. The imagery deliberately inverts the Genesis 3 pattern. Adam and Eve put on fig leaves — a self-generated, horizontal adjustment to a spiritual problem. Romans 13:14 commands a vertical adjustment: put on the Lord Jesus Christ. The history of human social reform is the history of sophisticated fig-leaf manufacture. The believer's calling is categorically different.

6. The lusts of the old sin nature (epithymiai) include socially approved pursuits. Epithymia in the plural encompasses any strong desire — moral or immoral — that diverts the believer from doctrine. A consuming civic project, a social crusade, a business ambition that consistently displaces doctrine: all of these qualify as provision made for the flesh. The old sin nature is as active in the realm of good as in the realm of evil.

7. Pronoia (foresight) identifies the cognitive dimension of carnality. Making provision for the old sin nature is not merely acting sinfully; it is planning, allocating attention, and directing mental energy toward the satisfaction of the old sin nature's appetites. The command to stop this is an appeal to redirect the mind's foresight toward the advance to maturity.

8. The filling of the Holy Spirit is the indispensable means of advance. Putting on the Lord Jesus Christ and not making provision for the old sin nature are both impossible apart from the filling of the Spirit. Rebound (1 John 1:9) is therefore embedded in the command as its operational prerequisite whenever fellowship is broken.

9. The royal family honor code is the application of maturity to horizontal relationships. Chapter 14 will detail how the strong believer and the weak believer relate to each other within the body of Christ. That code is not an independent ethical system; it is the natural outgrowth of maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Only the believer who has advanced through the maturity barrier has the doctrinal capacity to fulfill the honor code without either condemning the weak or capitulating to legalism.

10. Christianity does not sponsor social or political reform as its mission. The believer is not called to correct the evils of the devil's world but to glorify the Lord Jesus Christ through the advance to maturity. The stabilizing effect of a mature pivot is the divinely ordained mechanism by which God blesses and preserves a client nation — not legislation, not activism, and not institutional reform.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
endyō ενδύω endyō — to clothe oneself, to put on Verb: to dress oneself, to put on a garment. Used figuratively in Romans 13:14 for the believer's advance to maturity through sustained doctrine intake. The aorist middle imperative form emphasizes volitional participation in the result of the action.
alla αλλά alla — but, rather, on the contrary Strong adversative conjunction setting up a sharp contrast. In Romans 13:14 it contrasts the negative prohibitions of verse 13 with the single comprehensive positive command of verse 14.
pronoia πρόνοια pronoia — foresight, forethought, provision Noun from pro (before) + nous (mind). Denotes advance planning and the allocation of mental resources toward a goal. In Romans 13:14 it identifies the cognitive dimension of carnality: directing one's planning and attention toward the satisfaction of the old sin nature rather than toward advance to maturity.
sarx σάρξ sarx — flesh; old sin nature Noun with a range of meanings in Paul's letters. In Romans 13:14 it refers specifically to the old sin nature — the indwelling capacity for sin inherited at physical birth. The definite article functions as a possessive: 'your old sin nature.'
epithymia ἐπιθυμία epithymia — strong desire, craving, lust Noun denoting intense desire or craving. The plural epithymiai in Romans 13:14 encompasses the full range of distractions generated by the old sin nature — including socially approved pursuits and moral ambitions — that divert the believer from the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception.
poieō ποιέω poieō — to do, to make, to produce Common verb meaning to do, make, or produce. In Romans 13:14 it appears in the present middle imperative with the negative mē, yielding the imperative of prohibition: stop making provision. The present tense indicates an ongoing activity that is to cease.
Culminative Aorist A use of the Greek aorist tense that views a process or series of actions as a completed whole, emphasizing the result rather than the process itself. In Romans 13:14 the culminative aorist of endyō gathers the entire advance to maturity — daily doctrine intake over a lifetime — into one comprehensive result: maturity adjustment to the justice of God.
Royal Family Honor Code The operational standard governing the relationships of Church Age believers to one another and to unbelievers. It is the practical outworking of maximum doctrine resident in the soul and is treated in detail in Romans 14. The honor code is flexible in its application to life while remaining inflexible in its doctrinal foundations.
Pivot The body of mature believers within a national entity whose adjustment to the justice of God sustains divine blessing on that nation. The pivot is the primary mechanism by which God preserves a client nation and maintains the freedom necessary for evangelism and spiritual growth.
